# Overview

In Exercise 6, townships were grouped into regions by the similarity of their ICT rates. In this
exercise, accessibility is measured for every part of Singapore: how easily the residents of each
part can reach one of the 120 eldercare centres in the government's list of eldercare services.

On slide 3, accessibility is "the measure of the capacity of a location to be reached from, or to be
reached by, different locations", the definition of Rodrigue et al. (2013). Every measure in this
exercise combines demand, supply and the cost of travel:

- the demand at each place, the number of people who may use the service;
- the supply at each service location, the amount of service available;
- the cost of travel between each place and each service location, here the network distance along
  the roads.

**Part 1** is a reproduction of r4gdsa chapter 17, which computes three measures with the `ac()`
function of the `SpatialAcc` package: Hansen's potential model, the kernel density two-step floating
catchment area method (KD2SFCA) and the spatial accessibility measure (SAM). In **Part 2**, the
output of `ac()` is compared with the formulas on the Lesson 7 slides and in the readings, and the
distance matrix is checked. The 2SFCA and E2SFCA methods of slides 24 to 28 are added, and the
constant demand of the chapter is replaced with the number of residents aged 65 and over.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

## Sources

The hands-on exercise for Lesson 7 is this chapter:

- [Chapter 17: Modelling Geographical Accessibility](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap17.html)

The Lesson 7 outline lists four readings for before the lesson.

| Reading | What it contributes | Used in |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|----------------------|
| **Long (2017)**, "Modelling Accessibility", GIS&T Body of Knowledge | Network space and network distance; four classes of accessibility measure; the remark that gravity-based measures have no clear definition of a high or low value, so "all analysis must be relative"; aggregation of accessibility to regions | 3.1, 4.1, 4.6 |
| **Hansen (1959)**, *Accessibility and Residential Growth* | Accessibility as the sum of the opportunities at each zone divided by the separation raised to an exponent, and exponents of 2.2 to 3.0 by trip purpose | 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 4.2, 4.3 |
| **Luo and Wang (2003)**, "Measures of spatial accessibility to health care in a GIS environment" | The two steps of 2SFCA; 2SFCA as a special case of the gravity model with competition; the population-weighted mean of the accessibility scores equals the ratio of total supply to total demand; a larger catchment gives smoother scores | 3.1, 3.2, 3.4, 4.2 to 4.6 |
| **Luo and Qi (2009)**, "An enhanced two-step floating catchment area (E2SFCA) method" | Three travel zones within the catchment, with weights from a Gaussian function | 4.2 to 4.6 |

The outline links Hansen (1959) to a PDF at MIT. The PDF is Hansen's master's thesis of 1959, which
contains the accessibility model and the exponents used on this page. The article named on the
outline, "How Accessibility Shapes Land Use", is a summary of the thesis, published in the *Journal
of the American Institute of Planners* in 1959.

Of the six references the outline also lists, the following are used on this page:

| Reference | What it contributes | Used in |
|----------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|------------------|
| **Polzin, Borges and Coelho (2014)**, "An extended kernel density two-step floating catchment area method" | KD2SFCA as defined by Dai and Wang (2011), with the Epanechnikov kernel | 3.2, 4.2 to 4.5 |
| **Cheng et al. (2016)**, "Spatial difference analysis for accessibility to high level hospitals based on travel time in Shenzhen, China" | KD2SFCA with a Gaussian kernel whose width is set so that the weight at the catchment edge is 0.05 | 3.2, 4.2 to 4.5 |
| **Rodrigue, Comtois and Slack (2013)**, *The Geography of Transport Systems*, "Transportation and Accessibility" | The definition of accessibility quoted on slide 3 | 1 |

Rich (1980) and Orpana and Lampinen (2003) cover potential models and spatial choice models in
general, as background reading for this page.

Slide 29 cites Kalogirou and Foley (2006) for SAM. The paper is cited on slide 29 only, and is used
in sections 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 4.1 to 4.3 and 4.5. Its first author wrote the `SpatialAcc` package.

The outline's "All About R" section links three packages. `SpatialAcc` is used throughout. The
`potential` package (Stewart's potential model) and the `accessibility` package compute families of
measure that `SpatialAcc` also computes. This page uses only `SpatialAcc`.

The Lesson 7 slide deck is dated 12 October 2026, with 29 numbered slides. Slide 2 lists the Stewart
and Hansen potential models, 2SFCA, KD2SFCA and SAM. Slides 19 and 20 give the formula of Stewart's
potential model. Slides 24 to 27 give the formulas of 2SFCA and E2SFCA, and slide 29 gives the
formula of SAM. The deck has no formula for the Hansen model or for KD2SFCA.

:::

## Differences from the chapter

| | The chapter | This page | Why | Where |
|-----------------|-----------------|--------------------|--------------------------------------|--------|
| **Distance matrix** | used as read | checked against straight-line distances | 159 hexagons have the same network distance to all 120 centres. One of them is 2SFCA's highest-scoring hexagon in Part 2 | 4.1 |
| **Order of rows and columns** | assumed | checked | `ac()` pairs row $i$ of the distance matrix with hexagon $i$ and column $j$ with centre $j$, by position only | 2.4.2 |
| **Long to wide** | `spread()` | `pivot_wider()` | According to the chapter's own note, `pivot_wider()` replaces `spread()`; both functions give the same matrix | 2.4.2 |
| **Hansen decay** | `power = 2` in the step-by-step code, `power = 0.5` in the single code chunk | `power = 2` in Part 1; `power = 2`, `power = 0.5` and a power function compared in Part 2 | `ac()` weights a centre by $e^{-\beta d}$, with $\beta$ = `power`. With `power = 2` and distances in kilometres, the weight halves every 347 m | 4.3 |
| **Capacity in the Hansen model** | a constant 100 | a constant 100 | With unequal capacities, `ac(family = "Hansen")` multiplies the weights by the capacities of the wrong centres | 4.3 |
| **KD2SFCA kernel** | `ac()` default | compared with the kernels of Dai and Wang (2011) and Cheng et al. (2016) | The kernel of `ac()` is $e^{-d^2}$. At 2 km from a centre, the weight is 0.018 | 4.4 |
| **2SFCA and E2SFCA** | not covered | computed | Slides 24 to 28 | 4.4 |
| **SAM** | `d0 = 5` | `d0 = 5`, noted as unused | The SAM formula has no catchment, and `ac()` uses `d0` only for 2SFCA and KD2SFCA. With a constant demand of 100, SAM is $\sum_j n_j / d_{ij}^2$ divided by 100 | 3.3.1, 4.3 |
| **Demand** | 100 in every hexagon | residents aged 65 and over from the 2020 census, added in Part 2 | 1,334 of the 3,125 hexagons have no resident aged 65 and over | 4.5 |
| **Region of a hexagon** | `st_join()` with `st_intersects` | one region for each hexagon, the one it overlaps most | The join returns one row per subzone a hexagon touches: 5,406 rows for 3,125 hexagons | 3.1.3, 4.6 |
| **Mean marker on the boxplots** | `fun.y = "mean"` | `fun = "mean"` | `fun.y` has been deprecated since `ggplot2` 3.3.0 | 3.1.3 |
| **Theme of the charts** | the `ggplot2` default | `theme_minimal()`, with the regions named in full | The default grey panel and the axis label `REGION_N` are harder to read than the maps on this page | 3.1.3, 3.2.3, 3.3.3 |

# Getting started

## Packages

The chapter's code loads `ggstatsplot` and `reshape2`, but the two packages are not used, so they
are left out on this page. `patchwork` is added to place maps side by side, and `knitr` to format
tables.

```{r}
pacman::p_load(sf, SpatialAcc, tmap, patchwork,
               knitr, tidyverse)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
pacman::p_load(...)                                       # pacman
```

- `p_load()` loads each package, and installs any that are missing.

| Package | Used for |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `sf` | reading the shapefiles, coordinate reference systems, spatial joins |
| `SpatialAcc` | `ac()`, the accessibility measures |
| `tmap` | maps |
| `patchwork` | placing several charts or maps in one figure |
| `knitr` | tables |
| `tidyverse` | reading and reshaping the distance matrix (`readr`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`), and `ggplot2` charts |
:::

## The data

Section 17.2 of the chapter lists four data sets, which are distributed with the exercise on eLearn.

| Data set | Format | Features | Contents |
|-------------------------|--------------|------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL` | ESRI shapefile | 323 polygons | URA Master Plan 2014 subzone boundaries, from data.gov.sg |
| `hexagons` | ESRI shapefile | 3,125 polygons | hexagons covering the main island, Jurong Island and Sentosa, made with `st_make_grid()` |
| `ELDERCARE` | ESRI shapefile | 120 points | eldercare services, from data.gov.sg |
| `OD_Matrix` | CSV | 375,000 rows, 6 fields | network distance in metres from every hexagon to every centre |

According to the chapter, `hexagons`, `ELDERCARE` and `OD_Matrix` were prepared by Prof. Kam Tin
Seong for teaching and research, and may be used for this hands-on exercise. Use of the three data
sets for any other purpose requires the approval of Prof. Kam.

## Geospatial data

### Reading the three layers

The three layers have separate roles in the computation of Part 1:

| Object | Layer | One feature is | Used for |
|----------|----------------------|------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `hexagons` | `hexagons` | a hexagon of the main island, Jurong Island or Sentosa | demand in `ac()` (section 2.3.3) and rows of the distance matrix (section 2.4); unit of the Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM scores (sections 3.1 to 3.3) |
| `eldercare` | `ELDERCARE` | an eldercare service, with its postal code and address | supply in `ac()` (section 2.3.3) and columns of the distance matrix (section 2.4); red points on the maps of sections 3.1.2, 3.2.2 and 3.3.2 |
| `mpsz` | `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL` | a subzone of the URA Master Plan 2014, with its planning area and region | region of each hexagon, for the boxplots of sections 3.1.3, 3.2.3 and 3.3.3 |

```{r}
#| results: hide
mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL")
hexagons <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                    layer = "hexagons")
eldercare <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                     layer = "ELDERCARE")
```

```{r}
tibble(layer = c("mpsz", "hexagons", "eldercare"),
       features = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(hexagons), nrow(eldercare)),
       geometry = c(as.character(st_geometry_type(mpsz, by_geometry = FALSE)),
                    as.character(st_geometry_type(hexagons, by_geometry = FALSE)),
                    as.character(st_geometry_type(eldercare, by_geometry = FALSE))),
       epsg = c(st_crs(mpsz)$epsg, st_crs(hexagons)$epsg, st_crs(eldercare)$epsg)) |>
  kable()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
st_read(dsn, layer)                                       # sf
st_geometry_type(x, by_geometry = FALSE)                  # sf
st_crs(x)$epsg                                            # sf
tibble(...)                                               # tibble
kable(x, digits)                                          # knitr
```

- `st_read()` reads the shapefile named by `layer` from the folder `dsn` into a simple feature data
  frame. `results: hide` suppresses the report that `st_read()` prints for each file.
- `st_geometry_type(by_geometry = FALSE)` returns one geometry type for the whole layer.
- `st_crs()$epsg` returns the EPSG code of the coordinate reference system, or `NA` when the file
  does not contain one.
- `tibble()` builds a data frame from vectors of equal length, one column for each argument. Here
  the table has one row for each layer.
- `kable()` prints a data frame as a formatted table. The other tables on this page are also printed
  with `kable()`. Where `digits` is given, it rounds the numbers.
:::

The subzones have no EPSG code: their projection file describes SVY21 by its parameters only. The
hexagons and the eldercare centres are already in SVY21 with EPSG code 3414.

The map below shows the hexagons, the subzone boundaries and the eldercare centres together.

Five subzones have no hexagon: the North-Eastern Islands (Pulau Ubin and Pulau Tekong), Pulau
Seletar, Sudong, Semakau and the Southern Group. Of the 120 centres, 61 are in the Central Region,
which has 136 km² of the 781 km² of land in the subzone layer. The West Region, with 257 km², has 20
centres.

### Coordinate reference system

```{r}
mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
eldercare <- st_transform(eldercare, 3414)
hexagons <- st_transform(hexagons, 3414)

st_crs(mpsz)$epsg
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
st_transform(x, crs)                                      # sf
```

- `st_transform()` converts the coordinates of `x` to the coordinate reference system `crs`, here
  EPSG:3414, SVY21 / Singapore TM. For `hexagons` and `eldercare`, which are already in EPSG:3414,
  the call changes nothing. For `mpsz`, the call keeps the SVY21 projection and adds the EPSG code.
:::

The chapter text names the subzone layer `MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL` and the transformed object
`mpsz_svy21`. The chapter's code reads the layer `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL` into the object `mpsz`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Hexagons as the spatial unit

On slides 9 to 11, hexagons are the spatial unit. Administrative units such as subzones have shapes
and sizes set by planning decisions. Every hexagon has the same area. Of the regular polygons that
tile a plane, the hexagon is the closest to a circle.

```{r}
#| echo: false
hex_area <- as.numeric(st_area(hexagons[1, ]))
hex_side <- sqrt(2 * hex_area / (3 * sqrt(3)))
hex_apothem <- hex_side * sqrt(3) / 2
```

Each hexagon covers `r format(round(hex_area), big.mark = ",")` m². Its sides
are `r round(hex_side, 1)` m long, and the distance from its centre to the middle of each side
is `r round(hex_apothem)` m. The "250m radius" of section 17.2 is that distance. The centres of two
neighbouring hexagons are 500 m apart.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
amk <- mpsz |> filter(PLN_AREA_N == "ANG MO KIO")
amk_hex <- hexagons[st_intersects(hexagons, st_union(amk), sparse = FALSE)[, 1], ]
tm_shape(amk_hex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey50") +
tm_shape(amk) +
  tm_borders(col = "steelblue", lwd = 1.5) +
tm_shape(st_filter(eldercare, st_union(amk))) +
  tm_dots(fill = "red", size = 0.4) +
  tm_title("Ang Mo Kio: subzones (blue) and hexagons (grey), eldercare centres in red") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
```

The hexagons are the units of demand in every measure on this page. The demand of a hexagon is
placed at its centre point. The distance to each eldercare centre is measured from that point.
:::

### Demand and capacity

The layers read in section 2.3.1 have no field for the demand of a hexagon or the capacity of a
centre. The code below adds a `demand` column to `hexagons` and a `capacity` column to `eldercare`.
It also keeps only the identifier `fid` of `hexagons` and `eldercare`, and the postal code of each
centre.

```{r}
eldercare <- eldercare |>
  select(fid, ADDRESSPOS) |>
  mutate(capacity = 100)

hexagons <- hexagons |>
  select(fid) |>
  mutate(demand = 100)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
select(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
mutate(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
```

- `select()` keeps the identifier `fid` of each layer, and the postal code of each centre. The
  geometry column is kept by `sf` without being named.
- `mutate()` adds a constant column to each layer: a capacity of 100 for each centre, and a demand
  of 100 for each hexagon.

In the chapter, the same value is used for every hexagon and every centre "for the purpose of this
hands-on exercise", with a note that the actual demand and capacity should be used in practice. The
`ELDERCARE` layer has no field on the size of a centre, so the capacity stays at 100 on this page.
With the same demand in every hexagon and the same capacity at every centre, the Hansen, KD2SFCA and
SAM scores depend only on the distances in the distance matrix.

## Distance matrix

### Reading the distance matrix

```{r}
ODMatrix <- read_csv("data/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv",
                     skip = 0)
glimpse(ODMatrix)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
read_csv(file, skip)                                      # readr
glimpse(x)                                                # dplyr
```

- `read_csv()` reads the file into a tibble. With the default `skip = 0`, reading starts at the
  first line.
- `glimpse()` prints the number of rows and columns, and the type and first values of each column.
:::

The file has one row per pair of hexagon and eldercare centre: 3,125 hexagons × 120 centres
= `r format(nrow(ODMatrix), big.mark = ",")` rows.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fields of the distance matrix

Each row gives the cost of travel, in metres, from the centre of one hexagon to one eldercare
centre, divided into these parts:

| Field | Distance |
|--------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `entry_cost` | from the centre of the hexagon to the nearest road |
| `network_cost` | along the road network |
| `exit_cost` | from the road to the eldercare centre |
| `total_cost` | the sum of `entry_cost`, `network_cost` and `exit_cost` |

The invented street map below draws the `entry_cost`, `network_cost` and `exit_cost` of one pair of
hexagon and centre as three coloured lines.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.6
fd_unit <- 250                                              # metres per grid unit
fd_streets <- bind_rows(tibble(x = 0.3, xend = 10.2, y = c(1, 3.5, 6), yend = y),
                        tibble(x = c(1, 4, 7, 9.5), xend = x, y = 0.3, yend = 6.7))
fd_parts <- tribble(
  ~field,         ~x,  ~y,  ~xend, ~yend,
  "entry_cost",   2.5, 4.6, 2.5,   3.5,
  "network_cost", 2.5, 3.5, 7,     3.5,
  "network_cost", 7,   3.5, 7,     1,
  "network_cost", 7,   1,   8.3,   1,
  "exit_cost",    8.3, 1,   8.3,   1.6) |>
  mutate(len = sqrt((xend - x)^2 + (yend - y)^2))
fd_m <- tapply(fd_parts$len, fd_parts$field, sum) * fd_unit
fd_col <- c(entry_cost = "#e6550d", network_cost = "grey10", exit_cost = "#756bb1")
fd_lab <- tribble(
  ~field,         ~x,   ~y,   ~hjust,
  "entry_cost",   2.3,  4.0,  1,
  "network_cost", 5.5,  4.0,  0.5,
  "exit_cost",    8.75, 1.35, 0) |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("%s\n%s m", field, format(fd_m[field], big.mark = ",")))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 10.5, ymin = 0, ymax = 7.6, fill = "white", colour = "grey65") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.2, y = 7.4, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 4.3,
           label = sprintf("total_cost = %s + %s + %s = %s m",
                           format(fd_m["entry_cost"], big.mark = ","),
                           format(fd_m["network_cost"], big.mark = ","),
                           format(fd_m["exit_cost"], big.mark = ","),
                           format(sum(fd_m), big.mark = ","))) +
  geom_segment(data = fd_streets, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "grey85",
               linewidth = 3.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = 2.5, y = 4.6, xend = 8.3, yend = 1.6, colour = "grey55",
           linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 5.2, y = 2.95, angle = -27, size = 3.3, colour = "grey45",
           label = "straight line: not in the file") +
  geom_segment(data = fd_parts, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = field),
               linewidth = 2, lineend = "round") +
  geom_polygon(data = tibble(a = seq(0, 300, by = 60) * pi / 180,
                             x = 2.5 + 0.45 * cos(a), y = 4.6 + 0.45 * sin(a)),
               aes(x, y), fill = "#a1d99b", colour = "grey30", alpha = 0.8) +
  annotate("point", x = 2.5, y = 4.6, size = 2.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.5, y = 5.3, label = "centre of the hexagon", size = 3.6) +
  annotate("point", x = 8.3, y = 1.6, shape = 21, size = 8, fill = "#3182bd", colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 8.3, y = 2.35, label = "eldercare centre", size = 3.6) +
  geom_label(data = fd_lab, aes(x, y, label = label, colour = field, hjust = hjust),
             size = 3.6, lineheight = 0.9, fontface = "bold", fill = "white", linewidth = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 10.2, y = 6.35, hjust = 1, size = 3.3, colour = "grey45",
           label = "grey bands: roads") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = fd_col, guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 10.5), ylim = c(0, 7.6), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void()
```

The table shows the first three rows of the file, which give the distances from hexagon 1 to the
first three centres.

```{r}
#| echo: false
ODMatrix |>
  filter(origin_id == 1, destination_id %in% 1:3) |>
  kable(digits = 1)
```

Kalogirou and Foley (2006), the source of SAM, computed their distances in the same three parts:
from the centroid of each district to the nearest node of the road network, along the network, and
from the network to the hospital. Long (2017, section 2.2) gives the reason for distances along the
network: "most human movement occurs along a spatial network consisting of roads, railways, and
paths". Slide 6 shows the straight-line ("Cartesian") distance and the network distance of the same
trip.
:::

### From long to wide

`ODMatrix` has one row for each pair of hexagon and eldercare centre. `ac()` takes a matrix with one
row for each hexagon and one column for each centre. The chapter's code uses `spread()`, with a note
that `pivot_wider()` has replaced it since `tidyr` 1.0.

```{r}
distmat <- ODMatrix |>
  select(origin_id, destination_id, total_cost) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = destination_id,
              values_from = total_cost)

c(rows_match = identical(distmat$origin_id, hexagons$fid),
  cols_match = identical(as.numeric(names(distmat)[-1]),
                         as.numeric(eldercare$fid)))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
pivot_wider(data, names_from, values_from)                # tidyr
identical(x, y)                                           # base R
```

- `select()` keeps the three columns needed: the hexagon, the centre and the total distance.
- `pivot_wider()` makes one column for each value of `destination_id`, named by that value, and
  fills it with the `total_cost` of each hexagon to that centre. The result has one row for each
  `origin_id`.
- `identical()` checks that the rows are in the order of `hexagons$fid`, and that the column names
  are in the order of `eldercare$fid`.

In the invented example below, two hexagons and three centres make six pairs of hexagon and centre,
one row each. Each centre has its own colour. `pivot_wider()` places each value in the column of its
centre and the row of its hexagon.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
pw_col <- c(`1` = "#fdd0a2", `2` = "#c6dbef", `3` = "#dadaeb")
pw_long <- tibble(origin_id = rep(1:2, each = 3), destination_id = rep(1:3, 2),
                  total_cost = c(2.1, 4.5, 1.8, 2.3, 4.8, 2.0))
pw_lx <- c(1, 2.65, 4.3)                                  # columns of the long table
pw_wx <- c(7.9, 9.15, 10.4, 11.65)                        # columns of the wide table
pw_cells <- bind_rows(
  tibble(x = rep(pw_lx, each = 6), y = rep(6:1, 3), w = 1.6, dest = rep(pw_long$destination_id, 3),
         label = c(pw_long$origin_id, pw_long$destination_id, format(pw_long$total_cost))),
  tibble(x = rep(pw_wx, each = 2), y = rep(c(6, 5), 4), w = 1.2, dest = c(NA, NA, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3),
         label = c("1", "2", format(pw_long$total_cost[c(1, 4, 2, 5, 3, 6)]))))
pw_head <- tibble(x = c(pw_lx, pw_wx), y = 7, w = c(1.6, 1.6, 1.6, 1.2, 1.2, 1.2, 1.2),
                  dest = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, 1, 2, 3),
                  label = c("origin_id", "destination_id", "total_cost", "origin_id", "1", "2", "3"))
ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = bind_rows(pw_cells, pw_head), aes(x, y, width = w, fill = factor(dest)),
            colour = "white", linewidth = 1, height = 0.95) +
  geom_text(data = pw_cells, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 4) +
  geom_text(data = pw_head, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("segment", x = 5.4, xend = 7.0, y = 5.5, yend = 5.5, linewidth = 1.2,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.2, y = 6.1, label = "pivot_wider()", size = 3.7, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.65, y = 7.85, label = "Before: one row per pair", size = 4,
           fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 9.8, y = 7.85, label = "After: one row per hexagon,\none column per centre",
           size = 4, fontface = "bold", lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pw_col, na.value = "grey92", guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(ratio = 0.7, xlim = c(0.1, 12.4), ylim = c(0.4, 8.4)) +
  theme_void()
```

`identical()` compares two vectors position by position, and returns `TRUE` only when every position
holds the same value. The table shows the first positions of the column names of `distmat` and of
`eldercare$fid`.

| | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th | 7th | … |
|------------------------------------|------|------|------|------|------|------|------|------|
| column names of `distmat` | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 8 | … |
| `eldercare$fid` | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 8 | … |
| the same names sorted as text | 1 | **10** | **100** | **101** | **103** | **104** | **105** | … |

The column names of `distmat` and `eldercare$fid` are the same at every position, so `identical()`
returns `TRUE`. If the columns had been sorted as text, `identical()` would return `FALSE`, because
of the bold values. Then `ac()` would pair the second column, centre 10, with the capacity of
centre 2.
:::

`ac()` matches the matrix to the demand and the capacity by position: row $i$ to the $i$-th hexagon,
column $j$ to the $j$-th centre. The chapter's code includes no check of the order. The row check
and the column check return `TRUE`, so the rows of `distmat` follow the order of `hexagons` and the
columns follow the order of `eldercare`.

The 120 centres have identifiers between 1 and 133, with gaps. The columns of `distmat` follow the
order of the identifiers. After the first gap, the `fid` of the $j$-th centre is larger than $j$.

The first column of `distmat` holds `origin_id`. The column is removed, and the distances are
converted from metres to kilometres:

```{r}
distmat <- distmat |>
  select(-origin_id)

distmat_km <- as.matrix(distmat / 1000)
dim(distmat_km)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
as.matrix(x)                                              # base R
```

- `select(-origin_id)` drops the identifier column. In the chapter's code, the same step is
  `select(c(-c('origin_id')))`.
- Dividing the tibble by 1000 converts every distance from metres to kilometres. `as.matrix()`
  converts the result to a numeric matrix of 3,125 rows and 120 columns.
- `ac()` converts its argument `D` to a matrix in the first line of its source (section 4.2), so
  `ac()` gives the same scores for the tibble as for the matrix. The matrix is needed in sections
  4.3 and 4.4, where the distances are multiplied with `%*%`, which takes only matrices.
:::

According to the chapter, "the distance is measured in metre because SVY21 projected coordinate
system is used". The distances are along roads. Their unit comes from the network analysis that
produced the file. The conversion to kilometres changes the scores, because the Hansen and KD2SFCA
formulas in `ac()` raise e to a power of the distance (section 4.2): the same distance gives a
different weight in metres than in kilometres.

# Part 1: Chapter 17

This part follows r4gdsa [Chapter 17](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap17.html), sections 17.6 to
17.8. The Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM measures are each computed with `ac()`, joined to the hexagons,
mapped, and compared across the five regions of the Master Plan.

## Hansen's potential model

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## The potential model of Hansen (1959)

Hansen (1959) defines accessibility as "the potential of opportunities for interaction". The
definition comes from Stewart's potential of population (slide 19). Hansen describes that potential
as "directly proportional to the size of the group (activity level) and inversely proportional to
the distance or separation from that group". In Hansen's formula, the accessibility of zone $i$ is a
sum over all zones $j$. In this exercise, zone $i$ is a hexagon and zone $j$ is an eldercare centre:

$$A_i = \sum_j \frac{S_j}{T_{ij}^{\,x}} = \sum_j \frac{\text{capacity of centre } j}{(\text{road distance from hexagon } i \text{ to centre } j)^{x}}$$

$x$ is an exponent of distance. The contribution of a centre to the score of a hexagon increases
with the capacity of the centre and decreases with the distance between the centre and the hexagon.
A larger $x$ makes the contribution decrease faster with distance. In the speaker notes of slide 7,
the power function is traced to Newton's law of gravitation, the origin of the term gravity model.
According to the same notes, $x$ is large for grocery shopping, because people travel only a short
distance for groceries. For furniture shopping, $x$ is small, because people travel farther than for
groceries. The formula has no catchment, so every centre adds to the score of every hexagon, at any
distance.

The example below has one hexagon and three centres, with $x = 2$. The distances and capacities are
invented for this example. A line joins the hexagon to each centre. A wider line marks a larger term
$S_j/T_{ij}^2$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.5
hx <- tibble(centre = c("A", "B", "C"), d = c(1, 2, 2), capacity = c(100, 100, 400),
             angle = c(10, 135, 205) * pi / 180) |>
  mutate(x = d * cos(angle), y = d * sin(angle),
         term = capacity / d^2,
         label = sprintf("capacity %d, %d km\n%d / %d² = %g", capacity, d, capacity, d, term),
         label_x = x + c(0.35, -0.35, -0.45),
         hjust = c(0, 1, 1))
hx_rings <- expand_grid(r = c(1, 2), a = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 121)) |>
  mutate(x = r * cos(a), y = r * sin(a))
hx_hexagon <- tibble(a = seq(0, 300, by = 60) * pi / 180) |>
  mutate(x = 0.3 * cos(a), y = 0.3 * sin(a))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -4.9, xmax = 3.7, ymin = -2.9, ymax = 2.8, fill = "white",
           colour = "grey65") +
  annotate("text", x = -4.72, y = 2.66, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 4.3,
           label = sprintf("Score of the hexagon: %s = %g",
                           paste(hx$term, collapse = " + "), sum(hx$term))) +
  geom_path(data = hx_rings, aes(x, y, group = r), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey80") +
  annotate("text", x = (c(1, 2) + 0.2) * cos(-0.6), y = (c(1, 2) + 0.2) * sin(-0.6),
           label = c("1 km", "2 km"), colour = "grey50", size = 3.2) +
  geom_segment(data = hx, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y, linewidth = term),
               colour = "#3182bd", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_polygon(data = hx_hexagon, aes(x, y), fill = "#a1d99b", colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.48, label = "hexagon", size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(data = hx, aes(x, y, size = capacity), shape = 21, fill = "#3182bd", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_text(data = hx, aes(x, y - 0.04, label = centre), colour = "white",
            fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  geom_text(data = hx, aes(label_x, y, label = label, hjust = hjust), size = 3.6,
            lineheight = 0.9, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_linewidth(range = c(1, 3), guide = "none") +
  scale_size(range = c(9, 13), guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-4.9, 3.7), ylim = c(-2.9, 2.8)) +
  theme_void()
```

Centre B is twice as far from the hexagon as centre A, so its term is a quarter of the term of
centre A. Centre C is as far from the hexagon as centre B and has four times the capacity of centre
B, so the term of centre C is four times the term of centre B, the same as the term of centre A.

Slide 8 shows two forms of distance decay: the power function $\alpha / d^{\beta}$ and the
exponential function $\alpha e^{-\beta d}$. Hansen (1959, p. 5) uses the power function, which is
$1/d^2$ with $x = 2$. The `SpatialAcc` manual describes `power` as "the power of the separation
variable". The source of `ac()`, printed in section 4.2, computes the exponential function: with
`power = 2`, the value in the chapter's code, the weight is $e^{-2d}$, where $d$ is the road
distance in kilometres. The table compares the weights of $1/d^2$ and $e^{-2d}$, each relative to
the weight of a centre 1 km away:

| Function | Formula | 1 km | 2 km | 4 km | 8 km | Rule |
|----------------------|----------|------------|------------|------------|------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Hansen (1959), $x = 2$ | $1/d^2$ | 1 | $1/4$ | $1/16$ | $1/64$ | divided by 4 each time the distance doubles |
| `ac()`, `power = 2` | $e^{-2d}$ | 1 | $1/7$ | $1/403$ | $1/1{,}202{,}604$ | divided by $e^2 = 7.4$ for each extra kilometre |

The weight of the power function depends on the ratio of two distances, and the weight of the
exponential function on their difference.

:::

### Hansen scores from `ac()`

The distance matrix holds 375,000 road distances, one for each pair of hexagon and centre. The code
in this section turns them into one Hansen score for each of the 3,125 hexagons, and adds the scores
to the hexagons as `hexagon_Hansen`. The map of section 3.1.2 and the boxplots of section 3.1.3 are
drawn from `hexagon_Hansen`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## The `ac()` function

`ac()` is the function of the `SpatialAcc` package that computes the three measures of Part 1. The
package is by Stamatis Kalogirou, the first author of the SAM paper (Kalogirou and Foley, 2006). The
package manual titles `ac()` "Spatial Accessibility Measures". According to the manual, the function
"measures the accessibility of geographical areas to amenities". Accessibility is defined in section
1 as "the measure of the capacity of a location to be reached from, or to be reached by, different
locations".

```r
ac(p, n, D, d0, power = 2, family = "SAM")
```

| Argument | Meaning in the manual | In this exercise |
|--------------|----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| `p` | the demand for services in each location | the `demand` column of `hexagons` (section 2.3.3) |
| `n` | the supply of services in each location | the `capacity` column of `eldercare` (section 2.3.3) |
| `D` | a matrix of a quantity separating the demand from the supply | the road distance in kilometres, one row per hexagon and one column per centre (section 2.4) |
| `d0` | the threshold distance of the catchment | 5 km, used by KD2SFCA; the value is also passed to SAM but is not used in the SAM formula |
| `power` | the power of the separation variable | 2, the value in the chapter's code: the weight is $e^{-2d}$ in Hansen, $e^{-d^2}$ in KD2SFCA and $1/d^2$ in SAM |
| `family` | the accessibility measure | `"Hansen"`, `"KD2SFCA"` or `"SAM"` |

`ac()` returns one value for each element of `p`, here one score for each hexagon. The table below
shows how the capacity and the demand are used in the Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM measures:

| Measure | Capacity of a centre (`n`) | Demand of a hexagon (`p`) |
|-------------------|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Hansen (section 3.1) | factor in the weight of the centre | not used |
| KD2SFCA (section 3.2) | numerator of the ratio $R_j$ of the centre | denominator of $R_j$, summed over the hexagons in the catchment of the centre |
| SAM (section 3.3) | numerator of the term of the centre, $n_j / (p_i \, d_{ij}^{\beta})$ | divisor of the score of the hexagon |
:::

```{r}
acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 2,
                            family = "Hansen"))

colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
ac(p, n, D, d0, power, family)                            # SpatialAcc
bind_cols(...)                                            # dplyr
```

- `ac()` takes the demand of each hexagon (`p`), the capacity of each centre (`n`), the distance
  matrix (`D`), a catchment distance (`d0`), a decay parameter (`power`) and the measure (`family`).
  It returns one number for each row of `D`, the accessibility of that hexagon.
- `data.frame()` turns the vector into a one-column data frame, with a long column name made from
  the call. `colnames()` renames the column, and `as_tibble()` converts the data frame to a tibble.
- `bind_cols()` adds the column to `hexagons` by position, so that the $i$-th value goes to the
  $i$-th hexagon. The result keeps the geometry of `hexagons` and is still an `sf` object.
- `d0` is commented out because the Hansen measure in `ac()` has no catchment.

Before `bind_cols()`, `hexagons` and `acc_Hansen` each have 3,125 rows. The first score is in bold:

`hexagons`:

<div style="overflow-x: auto;">
<table class="table table-sm">
<tr><th>fid</th><th>demand</th><th>geometry</th></tr>
<tr><td>1</td><td>100</td><td>POLYGON ((2667.5 27506.3, …))</td></tr>
<tr><td>2</td><td>100</td><td>POLYGON ((2667.5 25006.3, …))</td></tr>
<tr><td>…</td><td>…</td><td>…</td></tr>
</table>
</div>

`acc_Hansen`:

The chapter's code then repeats the computation in a single code chunk, with `power = 0.5`.
`power = 2` and `power = 0.5` give different scores (section 4.3).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## The Hansen formula in `ac()`

```{r}
#| echo: false
half_km <- log(2) / 2
```

For each hexagon $i$, `ac(family = "Hansen")` adds up the capacity of every centre $j$, each
multiplied by a weight that falls exponentially with distance (exponential decay, slide 8):

$$A_i = \sum_j n_j \, e^{-\beta d_{ij}} = \sum_j (\text{capacity of centre } j) \times (\text{distance weight of centre } j)$$

where the distance weight is $e^{-\beta d}$, $\beta$ is `power` and $d$ is the road distance in
kilometres. Every centre contributes to the sum, at any distance. The figure below shows invented
centres along one road from a hexagon, at 0 m, 347 m, 1 km, 2 km and 3 km, and at the median road
distance of all pairs of hexagon and centre in the data, `r round(median(distmat_km), 1)` km.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.5
med_km <- median(distmat_km)
wt <- tibble(d = c(0, log(2) / 2, 1, 2, 3, med_km),
             pos = c(0, log(2) / 2, 1, 2, 3, 4.4)) |>
  mutate(w = exp(-2 * d),
         d_lab = if_else(d < 1, sprintf("%.0f m", d * 1000), sprintf("%.1f km", d)),
         w_lab = if_else(w > 1e-4, as.character(signif(w, 3)), "about~10^-15"))
ggplot(wt) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.35, xmax = 4.95, ymin = -0.45, ymax = 1.8, fill = "white",
           colour = "grey65") +
  annotate("text", x = -0.22, y = 1.7, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 4.3,
           label = "Weight of a centre in ac(family = \"Hansen\"), power = 2") +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 3.5, y = 0, yend = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = 4.0, xend = 4.7, y = 0, yend = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.75, y = 0, label = "//", size = 5, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = pos - 0.07, xmax = pos + 0.07, ymin = 0.12, ymax = 0.12 + w),
            fill = "#3182bd") +
  geom_text(aes(pos, 0.12 + w, label = w_lab), vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5, parse = TRUE) +
  geom_point(data = filter(wt, d > 0), aes(pos, 0), shape = 21, size = 5, fill = "#3182bd", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_polygon(data = tibble(a = seq(0, 300, by = 60) * pi / 180,
                             x = 0.1 * cos(a), y = 0.1 * sin(a)),
               aes(x, y), fill = "#a1d99b", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_text(aes(pos, -0.17, label = d_lab), size = 3.4, colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -0.31, label = "hexagon", size = 3.3) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.4, y = -0.31, label = "median distance", size = 3.3,
           colour = "grey30") +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-0.35, 4.95), ylim = c(-0.45, 1.8)) +
  theme_void()
```

With $\beta = 2$, the weight is 1 for a centre at the hexagon and halves
every `r round(half_km * 1000)` m. A centre 1 km away has a weight of `r round(exp(-2), 3)`. A
centre at the median distance has a weight of about $10^{-15}$.

The weight $e^{-\beta d}$ falls faster with distance as $\beta$ increases (chart below, as on slide
8). The chapter's code uses $\beta = 2$, drawn as the thick line.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
decay_chart <- function(curves, x_title = "road distance d (km)", y_title = "weight") {
  p <- plotly::plot_ly()
  for (k in unique(curves$curve)) {
    cv <- curves[curves$curve == k, ]
    p <- plotly::add_lines(p, data = cv, x = ~d, y = ~w, name = k,
                           line = list(width = if (cv$main[1]) 4 else 2,
                                       dash = if (cv$step[1]) "dash" else "solid"),
                           hovertemplate = paste0(k, "<br>d = %{x:.2f} km<br>weight = %{y:.4g}",
                                                  "<extra></extra>"))
  }
  plotly::layout(p, xaxis = list(title = x_title, zeroline = FALSE),
                 yaxis = list(title = y_title, rangemode = "tozero"),
                 legend = list(x = 0.72, y = 0.95),
                 hovermode = "closest")
}
expand_grid(beta = c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5), d = seq(0, 5, by = 0.02)) |>
  mutate(w = exp(-beta * d), curve = if_else(beta == 2, "β = 2 (chapter's code)", paste0("β = ", beta)),
         main = beta == 2, step = FALSE) |>
  decay_chart()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Limits of the Hansen measure

**No demand term.** The formula contains the capacity $n_j$ and the distance $d_{ij}$. It has no
demand term $p_i$. Two hexagons at the same distances from the same centres get the same score,
whether 10 or 10,000 residents aged 65 and over live in them. Luo and Wang (2003, equation 5) note
this limitation of Hansen's model: the model "considers only the 'supply side'". In the example
below, two invented hexagons are 1 km from the same centre, which has a capacity of 100.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
dm_hexagon <- function(cx, r = 0.62) {
  tibble(a = seq(0, 300, by = 60) * pi / 180) |>
    mutate(x = cx + r * cos(a), y = r * sin(a))
}
dm <- tibble(x = c(-1.9, 1.9), aged = c(10, 10000), fill = c("#d9f0d3", "#41ab5d"),
             ink = c("black", "white")) |>
  mutate(inside = sprintf("%s\nresidents\naged 65+", format(aged, big.mark = ",")))
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = dm, aes(x = x, y = 0, xend = 0, yend = 0), colour = "#3182bd",
               linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-0.95, 0.95), y = 0.17, label = "1 km", size = 4.5, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_polygon(data = dm_hexagon(dm$x[1]), aes(x, y), fill = dm$fill[1], colour = "grey30") +
  geom_polygon(data = dm_hexagon(dm$x[2]), aes(x, y), fill = dm$fill[2], colour = "grey30") +
  geom_text(data = dm, aes(x, 0, label = inside), colour = dm$ink, size = 4.6,
            lineheight = 0.9, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = dm$x, y = -0.88, size = 5, parse = TRUE,
           label = 'score*":"~100 %*% 0.135 == bold("13.5")') +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, shape = 21, size = 11, fill = "#3182bd", colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -0.03, label = "A", colour = "white", fontface = "bold",
           size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -0.4, label = "capacity 100", colour = "grey20", size = 4.5) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-2.8, 2.8), ylim = c(-1.05, 0.7)) +
  theme_void()
```

**No unit.** The score is a sum of weighted capacities, with no unit such as places per resident. A
score of 42.5 cannot be interpreted on its own. Scores can only be compared with each other, for
example to rank the hexagons. According to Long (2017, section 3), for such measures "there is no
clear definition of what a high or low value should be, all analysis must be relative".
:::

### Decile map of the Hansen scores

```{r}
mapex <- st_bbox(hexagons)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 7
tm_shape(hexagon_Hansen,
         bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "accHansen",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Hansen score"),
              col_alpha = 0.3) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: Hansen method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
st_bbox(obj)                                              # sf
tm_shape(shp, bbox)                                       # tmap
tm_polygons(fill, fill.scale, col_alpha)                  # tmap
tm_scale_intervals(style, n, values)                      # tmap
tm_dots(size, fill, col)                                  # tmap
tm_title(); tm_compass(); tm_scalebar(); tm_grid()        # tmap
```

- `st_bbox()` returns the bounding box of the hexagons: x
  from `r format(round(mapex[["xmin"]]), big.mark = ",")`
  to `r format(round(mapex[["xmax"]]), big.mark = ",")` m and y
  from `r format(round(mapex[["ymin"]]), big.mark = ",")`
  to `r format(round(mapex[["ymax"]]), big.mark = ",")` m in SVY21. Passed to
  `tm_shape(bbox = mapex)`, the box fixes the extent of the map. Each map in Part 1 shows the
  hexagons, which have this extent already, so the maps have the same extent without `bbox`.
- `tm_polygons(fill = "accHansen")` colours each hexagon by its score.
  `tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10)` divides the hexagons into ten classes of equal
  size (deciles), coloured from light to dark blue. `col_alpha = 0.3`, an addition to the chapter's
  code, lightens the hexagon borders.
- The second `tm_shape()` adds the centres, drawn by `tm_dots()` as red points with a black border.
- `tm_compass()`, `tm_scalebar()` and `tm_grid()` add a north arrow, a scale bar and a light
  coordinate grid.

In the invented example below, a layer has five hexagons. The maps in steps 3 and 4 show two of
them. In steps 3 and 4, the other three hexagons are faded because they are left out of the map.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 7.2
bb_hex <- tibble(id = 1:5, cx = c(1.2, 3.4, 2.2, 5.0, 1.6), cy = c(1.2, 1.6, 3.0, 3.4, 4.6),
                 in_map = id %in% c(2, 3))
bb_poly <- bb_hex |>
  rowwise() |>
  reframe(id, in_map, tibble(a = seq(0, 300, by = 60) * pi / 180) |>
            mutate(x = cx + 0.5 * cos(a), y = cy + 0.5 * sin(a)))
bb <- c(xmin = min(bb_poly$x), xmax = max(bb_poly$x), ymin = min(bb_poly$y), ymax = max(bb_poly$y))
bb_two <- bb_poly |>
  filter(in_map) |>
  summarise(xmin = min(x), xmax = max(x), ymin = min(y), ymax = max(y))
bb_panel <- function(title, faded = FALSE, box = NULL, box_col = "#3182bd", box_lty = "dashed",
                     box_labels = FALSE) {
  d <- bb_poly |> mutate(show = if (faded) in_map else TRUE)
  g <- ggplot() +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -0.3, xmax = 6.3, ymin = -0.2, ymax = 6.6, fill = "white",
             colour = "grey65") +
    annotate("text", x = -0.15, y = 6.45, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, label = title, size = 4,
             fontface = "bold", lineheight = 0.9) +
    geom_polygon(data = d, aes(x, y, group = id, alpha = show), fill = "#a1d99b", colour = "grey30")
  if (!is.null(box)) {
    g <- g + annotate("rect", xmin = box[["xmin"]], xmax = box[["xmax"]], ymin = box[["ymin"]],
                      ymax = box[["ymax"]], fill = NA, colour = box_col, linetype = box_lty,
                      linewidth = 1.1)
  }
  if (box_labels) {
    g <- g + annotate("text", size = 3.6, colour = "#08519c",
                      x = c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["xmax"]], 3.1, 3.1),
                      y = c(0.2, 0.2, bb[["ymin"]] - 0.25, bb[["ymax"]] + 0.25),
                      label = c("xmin", "xmax", "ymin", "ymax"))
  }
  g + scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1, `FALSE` = 0.15), guide = "none") +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.3, 6.3), ylim = c(-0.2, 6.6), expand = FALSE) +
    theme_void()
}
(bb_panel("1. A layer of five hexagons") |
   bb_panel("2. st_bbox() returns the box\naround the five hexagons", box = bb,
            box_labels = TRUE)) /
  (bb_panel("3. Map of two hexagons with\nbbox: the frame is the box", faded = TRUE, box = bb,
            box_col = "black", box_lty = "solid") |
   bb_panel("4. The same map without bbox:\nthe frame fits the two hexagons", faded = TRUE,
            box = unlist(bb_two), box_col = "black", box_lty = "solid"))
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
h_q <- quantile(hexagon_Hansen$accHansen, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
one_dist <- ODMatrix |>
  group_by(origin_id) |>
  summarise(k = n_distinct(total_cost)) |>
  filter(k == 1) |>
  pull(origin_id)
h_tab <- hexagon_Hansen |>
  mutate(near = apply(distmat_km, 1, min),
         n2 = rowSums(distmat_km <= 2),
         group = cut(accHansen, c(-Inf, h_q[1], h_q[3], Inf), c("bottom", "middle", "top")),
         one_dist = fid %in% one_dist) |>
  st_join(mpsz[c("PLN_AREA_N", "REGION_N")], join = st_intersects, largest = TRUE) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
sci <- function(x) {
  e <- floor(log10(x))
  sprintf("$%.1f \\times 10^{%d}$", x / 10^e, e)
}
near_range <- function(g) {
  d <- h_tab$near[h_tab$group == g]
  sprintf("%.2f to %.2f km (median %.2f)", min(d), max(d), median(d))
}
top_areas_of <- function(g) {
  h_tab |>
    filter(group == g) |>
    count(PLN_AREA_N, sort = TRUE) |>
    slice_head(n = 4) |>
    pull(PLN_AREA_N) |>
    str_to_title() |>
    paste(collapse = ", ")
}
h_max <- h_tab |> slice_max(accHansen, n = 1)
h_min <- h_tab |> slice_min(accHansen, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE)
bottom_near <- median(h_tab$near[h_tab$group == "bottom"])
score_median <- function(g) {
  m <- median(h_tab$accHansen[h_tab$group == g])
  if (m < 1e-3) sci(m) else as.character(signif(m, 3))
}
```

The classes are deciles: the 3,125 hexagons are sorted from the lowest score to the highest and
divided into ten groups of 312 or 313 hexagons, about 10% of the hexagons each. The colour of a
hexagon shows its decile. The table summarises the top decile, the middle 80% and the bottom decile:

| Hexagons | Hansen score | Nearest centre by road | Planning areas with the most hexagons |
|------------|-------------------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| Top 10% | `r signif(h_q[3], 3)` to `r round(max(h_tab$accHansen))` (median `r score_median("top")`) | `r near_range("top")` | `r top_areas_of("top")` |
| Middle 80% | `r sci(h_q[1])` to `r signif(h_q[3], 3)` (median `r score_median("middle")`) | `r near_range("middle")` | spread over all `r c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")[n_distinct(h_tab$REGION_N[h_tab$group == "middle"])]` regions |
| Bottom 10% | `r sci(min(h_tab$accHansen))` to `r sci(h_q[1])` (median `r score_median("bottom")`) | `r near_range("bottom")` | `r top_areas_of("bottom")` |

Of the `r sum(h_tab$group == "bottom")` hexagons in the bottom
decile, `r sum(h_tab$group == "bottom" & h_tab$one_dist)` have the same road distance to all 120
centres, an error in the distance matrix described in section 4.1.

The scores range over `r floor(log10(max(h_tab$accHansen) / min(h_tab$accHansen)))` orders of
magnitude, because the weight $e^{-2d}$ falls by a factor of 7.4 for each kilometre:

- The highest score, `r round(h_max$accHansen)`, is at a hexagon
  in `r str_to_title(h_max$PLN_AREA_N)`. Its nearest centre is `r round(h_max$near, 2)` km away by
  road, with a weight of `r round(exp(-2 * h_max$near), 2)`. The hexagon has `r h_max$n2` centres
  within 2 km by road.
- In the bottom decile, the median distance to the nearest centre is `r round(bottom_near, 2)` km. A
  centre at that distance has a weight of about `r sci(exp(-2 * bottom_near))`.
- The highest score is more than
  $10^{`r floor(log10(max(h_tab$accHansen) / min(h_tab$accHansen)))`}$ times the lowest score.
- The lowest score is shared by hexagons `r paste(h_min$fid, collapse = " and ")`
  in `r str_to_title(unique(h_min$PLN_AREA_N))`, each with the same road distance
  of `r round(h_min$near[1], 1)` km to every centre, the error described in section 4.1.

The map below labels the planning areas that have the most hexagons in the top and bottom deciles.

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r}
#| label: hansen-named-map

areas_of <- function(g) {
  h_tab |>
    filter(group == g) |>

}
named_areas <- mpsz |>

tm_shape(hexagon_Hansen, bbox = mapex) +

                                              values = "brewer.blues",

              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Decile of the\nHansen score"),

tm_shape(named_areas) +
```

### Hansen scores by region

```{r}
hexagon_Hansen <- st_join(hexagon_Hansen, mpsz,
                          join = st_intersects)
nrow(hexagon_Hansen)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
st_join(x, y, join = st_intersects)                       # sf
```

- `st_join()` adds the columns of `mpsz` to each hexagon whose geometry intersects a subzone. A
  hexagon that touches several subzones appears once for each of them.
:::

The join returns `r format(nrow(hexagon_Hansen), big.mark = ",")` rows for 3,125 hexagons. In the
boxplots below, a hexagon is counted once for each subzone it touches, so a hexagon on a subzone
boundary has more weight than a hexagon inside one.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(data = hexagon_Hansen,
       aes(y = log(accHansen),
           x = REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(stat = "summary",
             fun = "mean",
             colour = "red",
             size = 2) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) str_to_title(str_remove(x, " REGION"))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log of the Hansen score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
geom_boxplot()                                            # ggplot2
geom_point(stat = "summary", fun = "mean")                # ggplot2
```

- `aes(y = log(accHansen), x = REGION_N)` draws one box per region, on the natural logarithm of the
  score. Without the logarithm, every box would be a thin band near zero, because the scores range
  from below $10^{-20}$ to 198.
- `geom_point(stat = "summary", fun = "mean")` adds the mean of each region as a red point. The
  chapter's code uses `fun.y`, which `ggplot2` has replaced with `fun` since version 3.3.0.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
h_reg <- hexagon_Hansen |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(REGION_N) |>
  summarise(med = median(log(accHansen)),
            mean = mean(log(accHansen))) |>
  left_join(st_join(eldercare, mpsz["REGION_N"]) |>
              st_drop_geometry() |>
              count(REGION_N, name = "centres"),
            by = "REGION_N")
h_low <- hexagon_Hansen |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(accHansen < 1e-11) |>
  distinct(fid, REGION_N, PLN_AREA_N) |>
  mutate(one_dist = fid %in% one_dist)
reg_of <- \(r, v) h_reg[[v]][h_reg$REGION_N == r]
```

**Reading the chart.**

- The vertical axis is the natural logarithm of the score. A step of 1 on the axis is a factor of $e
  = 2.7$ on the original scale:

  | Log score | 5 | 0 | −5 | −25 | −50 |
  |-------------|-----------|---------|------------|------------------------|------------------------|
  | Score | `r round(exp(5))` | 1 | `r signif(exp(-5), 2)` | `r sci(exp(-25))` | `r sci(exp(-50))` |

- The black line in each box is the median. The box holds the middle half of the hexagons of the
  region. The red point is the mean.

**Regions.**

```{r}
#| echo: false
h_reg |>
  transmute(Region = str_to_title(REGION_N),
            `Eldercare centres` = centres,
            `Median log score` = round(med, 1),
            `Median score` = as.character(signif(exp(med), 2)),
            `Mean log score` = round(mean, 1)) |>
  kable()
```

- The Central Region has the highest median, `r round(reg_of("CENTRAL REGION", "med"), 1)` on the
  log scale (`r signif(exp(reg_of("CENTRAL REGION", "med")), 2)` on the original scale). The region
  has `r reg_of("CENTRAL REGION", "centres")` of the 120 centres.
- The West Region has the lowest median, `r round(reg_of("WEST REGION", "med"), 1)` on the log scale
  (`r signif(exp(reg_of("WEST REGION", "med")), 2)` on the original scale). The medians of the
  Central and West regions differ by a factor of
  about `r format(signif(exp(diff(range(h_reg$med))), 2), big.mark = ",")`.
- In every region, the mean is below the median. The log scores of each region have a long lower
  tail, which lowers the mean more than the median.
- Scores below $10^{-11}$ are in the East Region, mainly in Changi, and in the West Region, mainly
  in Tuas and Jurong Island. In the Central, North and North-East regions,
  the `r sum(h_low$REGION_N %in% c("CENTRAL REGION", "NORTH REGION", "NORTH-EAST REGION"))` hexagons
  with scores below $10^{-11}$ all have the same road distance to every centre, an error in the
  distance matrix described in section 4.1.

## Kernel density two-step floating catchment area (KD2SFCA)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Floating catchment area methods

KD2SFCA is the two-step floating catchment area method (2SFCA) with a distance weight inside the
catchment. On slide 24, 2SFCA is described as "a special case of a potential model". The table
explains the three terms in the name 2SFCA:

| Term | Meaning |
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| catchment | the area within a threshold distance $d_0$ of a point, here 5 km by road |
| floating | a catchment of the same size, drawn around one point after another |
| two-step | a catchment drawn twice: around every centre in step 1, then around every hexagon in step 2 |

In Luo and Wang (2003), the circle "floats from one centroid to another while its radius remains the
same". They trace 2SFCA to an earlier floating catchment area method with one step. That method
draws a circle around each residential location. The accessibility of the location is the ratio of
physicians to residents inside the circle, as if those physicians served only those residents. Luo
and Wang (2003) call this assumption "obviously faulty": a physician inside the circle also serves
residents outside it.

Slides 25 and 26 show the two steps of 2SFCA, with physicians as the supply and residents as the
demand. In this exercise, the supply is the capacity of a centre and the demand is the population of
a hexagon:

1. **Step 1, from each centre.** The ratio $R_j$ is the capacity of centre $j$ divided by the demand
   of all hexagons within $d_0$ of the centre. $R_j$ is the capacity per person in the catchment of
   the centre. When more people live in the catchment, $R_j$ is smaller.
2. **Step 2, from each hexagon.** The accessibility $A_i$ of hexagon $i$ is the sum of $R_j$ over
   all centres within $d_0$ of the hexagon.

The figure below shows the two steps with invented numbers and a catchment of 5 km. Hexagons and
centres outside the circle are faded, because they are left out of the calculation.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.3
fc_hexagon <- function(cx, cy, r = 0.6) {
  tibble(a = seq(0, 300, by = 60) * pi / 180) |>
    mutate(x = cx + r * cos(a), y = cy + r * sin(a))
}
fc_ring <- tibble(a = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 121)) |>
  mutate(x = 5 * cos(a), y = 5 * sin(a))
fc_panel <- function(hexes, centres, title, subtitle) {
  hex_poly <- hexes |>
    rowwise() |>
    reframe(id, inside, fc_hexagon(x, y))
  ggplot() +
    geom_polygon(data = fc_ring, aes(x, y), fill = "#deebf7", colour = "#3182bd",
                 linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.6) +
    annotate("text", x = 0, y = -5.5, label = "5 km", colour = "grey30", size = 3.5) +
    geom_polygon(data = hex_poly, aes(x, y, group = id, alpha = inside), fill = "#a1d99b",
                 colour = "grey30") +
    geom_text(data = hexes, aes(x, y - 1, label = label, alpha = inside), size = 3.5) +
    geom_point(data = centres, aes(x, y, alpha = inside), shape = 21, size = 10,
               fill = "#3182bd", colour = "grey30") +
    geom_text(data = centres, aes(x, y - 0.1, label = id), colour = "white",
              fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
    geom_text(data = centres, aes(x, y - 1, label = label, alpha = inside), colour = "grey20",
              size = 3.5) +
    scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1, `FALSE` = 0.3), guide = "none") +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(-8, 8), ylim = c(-6, 6)) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5))
}
step1 <- fc_panel(
  hexes = tibble(id = 1:4, x = c(-2.5, 2.5, 0, 6.6), y = c(1.5, 1.5, -3, 3),
                 label = "100 people", inside = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)),
  centres = tibble(id = "A", x = 0, y = 0, label = "capacity 3", inside = TRUE),
  title = "Step 1: a circle around each centre",
  subtitle = "ratio of centre A = 3 / (100 + 100 + 100) = 0.01")
step2 <- fc_panel(
  hexes = tibble(id = 1, x = 0, y = 0, label = "the hexagon", inside = TRUE),
  centres = tibble(id = c("A", "B", "C"), x = c(-2.8, 2.8, 6.6), y = c(1.8, 1.8, -3.5),
                   label = c("ratio 0.01", "ratio 0.02", "ratio 0.05"),
                   inside = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)),
  title = "Step 2: a circle around each hexagon",
  subtitle = "score of the hexagon = 0.01 + 0.02 = 0.03")
step1 | step2
```

In step 1, the 300 people within 5 km of centre A share its capacity of 3, so the ratio of centre A
is 0.01. In step 2, the score of the hexagon is the sum of the ratios of centres A and B, each
computed in step 1. Centre C is more than 5 km from the hexagon, so its ratio is left out of the
sum. In step 1, the 5 km circle is drawn around each centre in turn, and in step 2 around each
hexagon in turn.

The table compares the three measures:

| Measure | Catchment | Demand of the hexagons | Weight of a centre |
|--------------------|------------------|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Hansen (section 3.1) | none: every centre is used | not used | $e^{-\beta d}$, falls with distance |
| 2SFCA | $d_0$ | divides the capacity in step 1 | 1 inside the catchment, 0 outside |
| KD2SFCA | $d_0$ | divides the capacity in step 1 | falls with distance inside the catchment, 0 outside |

Polzin et al. (2014) attribute KD2SFCA to Dai and Wang (2011). In KD2SFCA, the demand in step 1 and
the ratios in step 2 are multiplied by the distance weight. A hexagon 500 m from a centre then has a
larger weight in the demand of the centre than a hexagon 4.8 km away. The ratio of the centre also
adds more to the score of the nearer hexagon.

In the example below, three invented hexagons share one centre with a capacity of 100. Hexagons 1
and 2 are 1 km from the centre. Hexagon 1 has 100 people. Hexagon 2 has 0 people in case X and 400
people in case Y. Hexagon 3, with 100 people, is 6 km from the centre, outside the 5 km catchment.
The figure is not to scale.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
hk_hexagon <- function(cx, r = 0.4) {
  tibble(a = seq(0, 300, by = 60) * pi / 180) |>
    mutate(x = cx + r * cos(a), y = r * sin(a))
}
hk <- tibble(id = 1:3, x = c(-2, 2, -6),
             people = c("100", "case X: 0 people\ncase Y: 400 people", "100"),
             fill = c("#d9f0d3", "#41ab5d", "#d9f0d3"))
ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = -6, xend = 2, y = 0, yend = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = -4.4, xend = -4.4, y = -1.2, yend = 1.2, colour = "#3182bd",
           linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = -4.4, y = 1.45, label = "edge of the 5 km catchment", colour = "#3182bd",
           size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-1, 1, -3.2), y = 0.3, label = c("1 km", "1 km", "6 km from A"),
           size = 3.2, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_polygon(data = hk_hexagon(hk$x[1]), aes(x, y), fill = hk$fill[1], colour = "grey30") +
  geom_polygon(data = hk_hexagon(hk$x[2]), aes(x, y), fill = hk$fill[2], colour = "grey30") +
  geom_polygon(data = hk_hexagon(hk$x[3]), aes(x, y), fill = hk$fill[3], colour = "grey30") +
  geom_text(data = hk, aes(x, y = 0, label = id), fontface = "bold", size = 3.5,
            colour = c("black", "white", "black")) +
  geom_text(data = hk, aes(x, y = -0.6, label = if_else(id == 2, people, paste(people, "people"))),
            size = 3.3, vjust = 1, lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, shape = 21, size = 8, fill = "#3182bd", colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -0.06, label = "A", colour = "white", fontface = "bold",
           size = 3.3) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -0.6, label = "capacity 100", colour = "grey20", size = 3.4,
           vjust = 1) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-7, 3), ylim = c(-1.2, 1.7)) +
  theme_void()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
hk_D <- matrix(c(1, 1, 6), ncol = 1)
hk_case <- function(people_2, family) {
  ac(c(100, people_2, 100), 100, hk_D, d0 = 5, power = 2, family = family)
}
hk_h0 <- hk_case(0, "Hansen");   hk_h4 <- hk_case(400, "Hansen")
hk_k0 <- hk_case(0, "KD2SFCA");  hk_k4 <- hk_case(400, "KD2SFCA")
hk_fmt <- \(x) if (x == 0) "0" else if (x < 0.01) sprintf("%.4f", x) else as.character(round(x, 2))
```

Case X: hexagon 2 is empty. Case Y: 400 people live in hexagon 2.

<div style="overflow-x: auto;">
<table class="table table-sm">
<tr><th rowspan="2">Hexagon</th><th colspan="2" style="text-align: center">Hansen, `power = 2`</th><th colspan="2" style="text-align: center">KD2SFCA, `d0 = 5`</th></tr>

<tr><td>3 (6 km from A)</td><td>`r hk_fmt(hk_h0[3])`</td><td>`r hk_fmt(hk_h4[3])`</td><td style="font-weight: bold">`r hk_fmt(hk_k0[3])`</td><td style="font-weight: bold">`r hk_fmt(hk_k4[3])`</td></tr>

- From case X to case Y, the Hansen score of hexagon 1 stays at `r hk_fmt(hk_h4[1])`.
- From case X to case Y, the KD2SFCA score of hexagon 1 falls from `r hk_fmt(hk_k0[1])`
  to `r hk_fmt(hk_k4[1])`, because in case Y the 500 people within the catchment share the capacity
  of 100.
- Hexagon 3 is 6 km from the centre, outside the catchment, so its KD2SFCA score is 0 in case X and
  in case Y. Its Hansen score is small, but above 0.

:::

### KD2SFCA scores from `ac()`

The code in this section computes one KD2SFCA score for each of the 3,125 hexagons, with a catchment
of 5 km, and adds the scores to the hexagons as `hexagon_KD2SFCA`. The map of section 3.2.2 and the
boxplots of section 3.2.3 are drawn from `hexagon_KD2SFCA`.

```{r}
acc_KD2SFCA <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                             eldercare$capacity,
                             distmat_km,
                             d0 = 5,
                             power = 2,
                             family = "KD2SFCA"))

colnames(acc_KD2SFCA) <- "accKD2SFCA"
acc_KD2SFCA <- as_tibble(acc_KD2SFCA)
hexagon_KD2SFCA <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_KD2SFCA)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- The call is the Hansen call of section 3.1.1 with `family = "KD2SFCA"` and a catchment of `d0 = 5`
  km. In the chapter, the chunk is described as calculating "Hansen's accessibility", a description
  copied from section 17.6, which covers the Hansen measure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## The 2SFCA formula and an example

Luo and Wang (2003, equations 3 and 4) write the two steps as

$$R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_{k:\, d_{kj} \le d_0} P_k} = \frac{\text{capacity of centre } j}{\text{demand of the hexagons within } d_0 \text{ of centre } j}$$

$$A_i = \sum_{j:\, d_{ij} \le d_0} R_j = \text{sum of } R_j \text{ over the centres within } d_0 \text{ of hexagon } i$$

where $S_j$ is the capacity of centre $j$ and $P_k$ is the demand of hexagon $k$. In an invented
example of four hexagons and two centres, centre A has a capacity of 1, centre B has a capacity of
3, and the catchment is 5 km:

```{r}
#| echo: false
toy_D <- matrix(c(1, 2, 4, 6,
                  6, 4, 2, 1), ncol = 2,
                dimnames = list(paste("hexagon", 1:4), c("A", "B")))
toy_p <- c(100, 200, 100, 100)
toy_n <- c(1, 3)
toy_R <- toy_n / colSums(toy_p * (toy_D <= 5))
toy_A <- as.vector((toy_D <= 5) %*% toy_R)
tibble(` ` = rownames(toy_D),
       `km to A` = toy_D[, 1], `km to B` = toy_D[, 2],
       demand = toy_p,
       `centres within 5 km` = c("A", "A, B", "A, B", "B"),
       `by hand` = toy_A,
       `ac(family = "2SFCA")` = ac(toy_p, toy_n, toy_D, d0 = 5, family = "2SFCA")) |>
  kable(digits = 4)
```

The scores from `ac()` are the same as the hand calculation for all four hexagons.

**Unit.** The scores have a unit: capacity per person.

**Average.** Luo and Wang (2003) show that the average of the scores, weighted by demand, equals the
total capacity divided by the total demand. In the example, $(100 \times 0.0025 + 200 \times 0.01 +
100 \times 0.01 + 100 \times 0.0075) / 500 = 0.008 = 4 / 500$. The same check is applied to the
eldercare data in section 4.4.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## The KD2SFCA formula in `ac()`

In KD2SFCA, step 1 and step 2 of 2SFCA are each weighted by a kernel that falls with distance.
According to the source of `ac()` (section 4.2), the kernel is $e^{-d^{\beta}}$, where $\beta$ is
`power`:

$$R_j = \frac{n_j}{\sum_{k:\, d_{kj} \le d_0} p_k \, e^{-d_{kj}^{\beta}}}, \qquad A_i = \sum_{j:\, d_{ij} \le d_0} R_j \, e^{-d_{ij}^{\beta}}$$

With `power = 2` and `d0 = 5`, a hexagon or centre inside the 5 km catchment has the weight
$e^{-d^2}$, with $d$ in kilometres. A hexagon or centre outside the catchment has the weight 0. The
figure below shows the weight at invented distances along one road from a hexagon.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.3
kd_w <- tibble(d = c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6)) |>
  mutate(w = if_else(d <= 5, exp(-d^2), 0),
         d_lab = if_else(d < 1, sprintf("%.0f m", d * 1000), sprintf("%g km", d)),
         e = floor(log10(pmax(w, 1e-300))),
         w_lab = case_when(w == 0 ~ "0",
                           w > 1e-4 ~ as.character(signif(w, 2)),
                           TRUE ~ sprintf("%.1f %%*%% 10^%s", w / 10^e, e)))
ggplot(kd_w) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.35, xmax = 6.55, ymin = -0.45, ymax = 1.8, fill = "white",
           colour = "grey65") +
  annotate("text", x = -0.22, y = 1.7, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 4.3,
           label = "Weight of a centre in ac(family = \"KD2SFCA\"), power = 2, d0 = 5") +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 6.4, y = 0, yend = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = 5.5, xend = 5.5, y = -0.05, yend = 1.15, colour = "#3182bd",
           linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 5.5, y = 1.22, label = "edge of the 5 km catchment", size = 3.2,
           colour = "#3182bd") +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = d - 0.08, xmax = d + 0.08, ymin = 0.12, ymax = 0.12 + w),
            fill = "#3182bd") +
  geom_text(aes(d, 0.12 + w, label = w_lab), vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5, parse = TRUE) +
  geom_point(data = filter(kd_w, d > 0), aes(d, 0), shape = 21, size = 5, fill = "#3182bd", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_polygon(data = tibble(a = seq(0, 300, by = 60) * pi / 180,
                             x = 0.1 * cos(a), y = 0.1 * sin(a)),
               aes(x, y), fill = "#a1d99b", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_text(aes(d, -0.17, label = d_lab), size = 3.4, colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -0.31, label = "hexagon", size = 3.3) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-0.35, 6.55), ylim = c(-0.45, 1.8)) +
  theme_void()
```

The weight is 0.37 at 1 km and 0.018 at 2 km. At 5 km, the edge of the catchment, it is $1.4 \times
10^{-11}$, and beyond 5 km it is 0.

The weight $e^{-d^{\beta}}$ is $e^{-1} = 0.37$ at 1 km for every $\beta$. A larger $\beta$ gives a
larger weight below 1 km and a smaller weight above it, and every weight is 0 beyond 5 km (chart
below; the dashed line is 2SFCA, with a weight of 1 inside the catchment).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
bind_rows(
  expand_grid(beta = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5), d = seq(0, 6, by = 0.02)) |>
    mutate(w = if_else(d <= 5, exp(-d^beta), 0),
           curve = if_else(beta == 2, "β = 2 (chapter's code)", paste0("β = ", beta)),
           main = beta == 2, step = FALSE),
  tibble(d = seq(0, 6, by = 0.02)) |>
    mutate(w = as.numeric(d <= 5), curve = "2SFCA (weight 1)", main = FALSE, step = TRUE)) |>
  decay_chart()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Limits of the kernel in `ac()`

**No width.** The kernel $e^{-d^2}$ has no parameter for its width, so its shape is the same for any
catchment. The weight is below 0.02 beyond 2 km, so a centre beyond 2 km has less than 2% of the
weight of a centre at the hexagon. The kernels of Dai and Wang (2011) and Cheng et al. (2016) are
scaled by the catchment (section 4.4).

**Unit of distance.** The weight depends on the unit of the distances. A centre 2 km away has a
weight of 0.018 with distances in kilometres, and a weight of 0 with distances in metres (section
4.2).
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
pa_of <- h_tab |> select(fid, PLN_AREA_N, REGION_N)
fmt <- function(x) if (x == 0) "0" else if (x < 1e-3) sci(x) else as.character(signif(x, 3))
group_near <- function(tab, g) {
  d <- tab$near[tab$group == g]
  sprintf("%.2f to %.2f km (median %.2f)", min(d), max(d), median(d))
}
group_score <- function(tab, var, g) {
  s <- tab[[var]][tab$group == g]
  sprintf("%s to %s (median %s)", fmt(min(s)), fmt(max(s)), fmt(median(s)))
}
group_areas <- function(tab, g) {
  tab |>
    filter(group == g) |>
    count(PLN_AREA_N, sort = TRUE) |>
    slice_head(n = 4) |>
    pull(PLN_AREA_N)
}
title_list <- \(x) paste(str_to_title(x), collapse = ", ")
n_regions <- \(tab, g) c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")[n_distinct(tab$REGION_N[tab$group == g])]
kd_tab <- hexagon_KD2SFCA |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(near = apply(distmat_km, 1, min),
         n1 = rowSums(distmat_km <= 1),
         group = case_when(accKD2SFCA == 0 ~ "zero",
                           accKD2SFCA >= quantile(accKD2SFCA, 0.9) ~ "top",
                           TRUE ~ "middle"),
         one_dist = fid %in% one_dist) |>
  left_join(pa_of, by = "fid")
kd_areas <- \(g) group_areas(kd_tab, g)
kd_zero <- sum(kd_tab$group == "zero")
kd_max <- kd_tab |> slice_max(accKD2SFCA, n = 1)
kd_mid_near <- median(kd_tab$near[kd_tab$group == "middle"])
```

The classes are deciles, as in section 3.1.2. Of the 3,125
hexagons, `r format(kd_zero, big.mark = ",")` (`r round(100 * kd_zero / 3125)`%) score exactly 0,
because no centre is within 5 km of them by road. The 10th to 40th percentiles are therefore all 0,
and the four lowest classes of the legend run from 0 to 0. The table lists three groups of hexagons:

| Hexagons | KD2SFCA score | Nearest centre by road | Planning areas with the most hexagons |
|----------------|-------------------------------------|-------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Top 10% | `r group_score(kd_tab, "accKD2SFCA", "top")` | `r group_near(kd_tab, "top")` | `r title_list(kd_areas("top"))` |
| Other scores above 0 | `r group_score(kd_tab, "accKD2SFCA", "middle")` | `r group_near(kd_tab, "middle")` | spread over all `r n_regions(kd_tab, "middle")` regions |
| Score 0 | 0 | `r group_near(kd_tab, "zero")` | `r title_list(kd_areas("zero"))` |

Of the `r format(kd_zero, big.mark = ",")` hexagons with a score of
0, `r sum(kd_tab$group == "zero" & kd_tab$one_dist)` have the same road distance to every centre, an
error in the distance matrix described in section 4.1.

The kernel $e^{-d^2}$ is below 0.02 beyond 2 km:

- The highest score, `r round(kd_max$accKD2SFCA, 2)`, is at a hexagon
  in `r str_to_title(kd_max$PLN_AREA_N)`. The hexagon has `r kd_max$n1` centres within 1 km by road.
- Among the other scores above 0, the median distance to the nearest centre
  is `r round(kd_mid_near, 2)` km. A centre at that distance has a weight of
  about `r sci(exp(-round(kd_mid_near, 2)^2))`.
- A hexagon with no centre within 5 km by road scores 0, however many centres are just beyond 5 km.

The map below shows the three groups of the table, and labels the planning areas that have the most
hexagons in the top 10% and with a score of 0.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Map

```{r}
#| label: kd2sfca-named-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6
label_areas <- function(areas) {
  mpsz |>
    filter(PLN_AREA_N %in% areas) |>
    group_by(PLN_AREA_N) |>
    summarise() |>
    st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON") |>
    st_cast("POLYGON") |>
    mutate(area = st_area(geometry)) |>
    group_by(PLN_AREA_N) |>
    slice_max(area, n = 1) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(label = str_to_title(PLN_AREA_N),
           label = if_else(PLN_AREA_N == "WESTERN ISLANDS",
                           "Jurong Island\n(Western Islands)", label))
}
kd_groups <- hexagon_KD2SFCA |>
  mutate(group = case_when(accKD2SFCA == 0 ~ "0",
                           accKD2SFCA >= quantile(accKD2SFCA, 0.9) ~ "top 10%",
                           TRUE ~ "above 0, below the top 10%"),
         group = factor(group, c("0", "above 0, below the top 10%", "top 10%")))
tm_shape(kd_groups, bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "group",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c("grey92", "#9ecae1", "#08519c")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "KD2SFCA score"),
              col_alpha = 0.3) +
tm_shape(label_areas(c(kd_areas("top"), kd_areas("zero")))) +
  tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 1.2) +
  tm_text("label", size = 0.75, fontface = "bold", bgcol = "white", bgcol_alpha = 0.75) +
  tm_title("Planning areas with the most hexagons in the top 10% and at 0") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)
```

```{r}

ggplot(data = hexagon_KD2SFCA,
       aes(y = accKD2SFCA,
```
