## Network distances: missing routes and the straight-line lower bound

In the network analysis of Kalogirou and Foley (2006, p. 55), no distance was found for some
electoral divisions, "primarily on islands". The 9,090 residents of those divisions, 0.23% of the
resident population of Ireland in the 2002 census, were left out of their model. In chapter 17,
`distmat_km` is used without a check for missing distances. A network distance follows the roads
(Long, 2017, section 2.2; slide 6), so it is at least as long as the straight line between the same
two points. Comparing each network distance with the straight-line distance of the same pair is an
extension of the course material, based on that definition.

The question for this section is whether the distances in `OD_Matrix.csv` satisfy two conditions: no
network distance is shorter than the straight line, and the distances from a hexagon to different
centres differ.

```{r}
hex_xy <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(hexagons)))
ctr_xy <- st_coordinates(eldercare)
euclid_km <- sqrt(outer(hex_xy[, 1], ctr_xy[, 1], "-")^2 +
                  outer(hex_xy[, 2], ctr_xy[, 2], "-")^2) / 1000
detour <- distmat_km / euclid_km

c(pairs = length(detour),
  median_ratio = median(detour),
  network_shorter = sum(detour < 1))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
st_centroid(x); st_coordinates(x)                         # sf
outer(X, Y, FUN = "-")                                    # base R
```

- `st_centroid()` returns the centre of each hexagon, and `st_coordinates()` returns the x and y of
  each centre in metres.
- `outer(X, Y, "-")` subtracts every coordinate of a centre from every coordinate of a hexagon, and
  returns a matrix of 3,125 hexagons by 120 centres. The straight-line distance is the square root
  of the sum of the squared x and y differences, divided by 1000 to give kilometres.
- `detour` divides each network distance by the straight-line distance of the same pair.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
n_short <- sum(detour < 1)
```

The median network distance is `r round(median(detour), 2)` times the straight-line distance. The
first condition fails for `r format(n_short, big.mark = ",")` of the 375,000 pairs of hexagon and
centre: their network distance is shorter than the straight line.

```{r}
od_check <- ODMatrix |>
  group_by(origin_id) |>
  summarise(distinct_costs = n_distinct(total_cost))

broken_fid <- od_check$origin_id[od_check$distinct_costs == 1]
length(broken_fid)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
n_distinct(x)                                             # dplyr
```

- For each hexagon, `n_distinct()` counts the different values of `total_cost` among its 120 rows. A
  hexagon with a different distance to each of the 120 centres has 120 distinct values of
  `total_cost`.
:::

Of the 3,125 hexagons, `r length(broken_fid)` have one value of `total_cost` for all 120 centres.

```{r}
centre_exit <- ODMatrix |>
  filter(!origin_id %in% broken_fid) |>
  distinct(destination_id, exit_cost)

ODMatrix |>
  filter(origin_id %in% broken_fid) |>
  distinct(origin_id, exit_cost) |>
  left_join(centre_exit, by = "exit_cost") |>
  count(destination_id)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `exit_cost` is the distance from the road to a centre, so each centre has one value, the same for
  every hexagon. `centre_exit` lists that value for each centre, from the hexagons with valid rows.
- The join matches the `exit_cost` of each of the 159 hexagons to the centre with that value, and
  `count()` counts the hexagons per centre.
:::

All 159 hexagons carry the exit cost of centre 133, the last centre in the file. Their rows hold the
distance to centre 133, repeated for every other centre. The pattern is consistent with a network
analysis in which no route was found from these hexagons, and their rows were filled with the result
for the last centre.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5.5
hexagons <- hexagons |>
  mutate(od_ok = !fid %in% broken_fid)
broken_pa <- st_join(st_centroid(filter(hexagons, !od_ok)),
                     mpsz["PLN_AREA_N"]) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(PLN_AREA_N, sort = TRUE)
broken_near <- sum(apply(euclid_km[!hexagons$od_ok, ], 1, min) <= 5)
tm_shape(hexagons, bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "od_ok",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c("firebrick", "grey92"),
                                                labels = c("one distance to all centres",
                                                           "distances vary")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Row in OD_Matrix"),
              col_alpha = 0.2) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.2, fill = "black") +
  tm_title("Hexagons with one network distance to all 120 centres") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
```

Of the 159 hexagons, `r broken_pa$n[1]` are in the Western Water Catchment and `r broken_pa$n[2]` in
the Southern Islands. The other `r 159 - broken_pa$n[1] - broken_pa$n[2]` are scattered along the
coast and the edges of the reservoirs. Of the 159, `r broken_near` have a centre within 5 km in a
straight line, so their KD2SFCA score of 0 in section 3.2 may be wrong. One hexagon, 1067, near
International Business Park, has a repeated distance of 4.97 km, so all 120 centres are inside its
catchment of 5 km.

In the rest of Part 2, the 159 hexagons are left out of every calculation and mapped in grey. The
accessibility measures are computed on the other 2,966 hexagons and their rows of the distance
matrix:

```{r}
ok <- hexagons$od_ok
D <- distmat_km[ok, ]
p100 <- hexagons$demand[ok]
n100 <- eldercare$capacity
dim(D)
```

## Formulas in `ac()`: code versus slides and readings

In section 3, `ac()` was called three times, for the Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM measures. No formula
for the three measures is given in chapter 17. The authors of the readings write out the formula of
each measure they compute: Hansen (1959, p. 5), Luo and Wang (2003, equations 3 to 6), Luo and Qi
(2009, equations 1 to 5), Polzin et al. (2014, equations 3 and 4), Cheng et al. (2016, equations 1
to 5) and Kalogirou and Foley (2006, p. 58). On the slides, formulas are given for Stewart's
potential model (slide 19), 2SFCA (slides 25 and 26), E2SFCA (slide 27) and SAM (slide 29). Slide 8
shows the two usual forms of distance decay: the power function $\alpha / d^{\beta}$ and the
exponential function $\alpha e^{-\beta d}$. The source of `ac()`, about 50 lines long, is printed by
typing the name of the function:

```{r}
SpatialAcc::ac
```

The table lists each value of the `family` argument of `ac()` beside its definition in the slides
and the readings.

| Family | Computed by `ac()` | In the slides or the readings | Difference |
|-----------|---------------------------|-------------------------------------|-------------------------|
| `Hansen` | $\sum_j n_j e^{-\beta d_{ij}}$ | Hansen (1959, p. 5): $\sum_j S_j / T_{ij}^{x}$; slide 19 (Stewart): $\sum_j M_j / d_{ij}^{\alpha}$ | exponential decay in `ac()`, power function in Hansen's thesis |
| `2SFCA` | $\sum_{j: d_{ij} \le d_0} n_j / \sum_{k: d_{kj} \le d_0} p_k$ | slides 25 and 26; Luo and Wang (2003, equations 3 and 4) | none |
| `KD2SFCA` | 2SFCA with each term multiplied by $e^{-d^{\beta}}$ | Dai and Wang (2011), according to Polzin et al. (2014, equation 4): $\tfrac{3}{4}(1 - (d/d_0)^2)$; Cheng et al. (2016, equation 3): $e^{-d^2/k}$ | the kernel of `ac()` has no width parameter, so its shape is the same for every $d_0$ |
| `SAM` | $\sum_j n_j / (p_i \, d_{ij}^{\beta})$ | slide 29: $\frac{1}{p_i} \sum_j n_j / (p_i \, d_{ij}^2)$ | $p_i$ appears once in `ac()` and twice on the slide; `d0` is not used |

Hansen's thesis says that "an exponential function of distance should be used", and then explains
that "the measurement of distance separating the various areas should be raised to some power". In
the thesis, the "exponential function of distance" is the distance raised to a power. `ac()`
computes the exponential function of slide 8, e raised to a multiple of the distance.

The chart shows the weight of each kernel on this page at each distance, together with the
distribution of the distance from each hexagon to its nearest centre.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Chart

```{r}
#| label: kernel-chart
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 9
k_cheng <- 5^2 / log(20)
near <- apply(D, 1, min)
near_med <- median(near)

kernels <- list(
  `Hansen, power = 2: exp(-2d)`         = \(d) exp(-2 * d),
  `Hansen, power = 0.5: exp(-0.5d)`     = \(d) exp(-0.5 * d),
  `power function: 1/d²`                = \(d) pmin(1, 1 / d^2),
  `KD2SFCA in ac(): exp(-d²)`           = \(d) exp(-d^2) * (d <= 5),
  `Epanechnikov, d0 = 5 km`             = \(d) (1 - (d / 5)^2) * (d <= 5),
  `Gaussian of Cheng et al., d0 = 5 km` = \(d) exp(-d^2 / k_cheng) * (d <= 5),
  `2SFCA, d0 = 5 km`                    = \(d) as.numeric(d <= 5))
k_col <- c("#08519c", "#6baed6", "#31a354", "#e6550d", "#fdae6b", "#756bb1", "#666666")
k_thick <- c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)  # the chapter's two kernels

d <- sort(c(seq(0, 10, by = 0.05), near_med))
p_decay <- plotly::plot_ly()
for (k in seq_along(kernels)) {
  name <- names(kernels)[k]
  p_decay <- p_decay |>
    plotly::add_lines(x = d, y = kernels[[k]](d), name = name, legendgroup = name,
                      line = list(color = k_col[k], width = if (k_thick[k]) 4 else 2,
                                  dash = if (k == 7) "dash" else "solid"),
                      hovertemplate = "%{y:.3g}") |>
    plotly::add_markers(x = near_med, y = kernels[[k]](near_med), name = name,
                        legendgroup = name, showlegend = FALSE,
                        marker = list(color = k_col[k], size = 10), hoverinfo = "skip")
}
median_line <- list(dash = "dot", color = "#4d4d4d", width = 1.5)
median_hover <- sprintf("median distance to the nearest centre: %.2f km", near_med)
p_decay <- p_decay |>
  plotly::add_lines(x = c(near_med, near_med), y = c(0, 1), line = median_line,
                    name = "median", showlegend = FALSE, hovertemplate = median_hover) |>
  plotly::layout(yaxis = list(title = "weight"))

bins <- tibble(d = near) |>
  count(lo = floor(d / 0.25) * 0.25) |>
  mutate(range = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f km", lo, lo + 0.25))
p_near <- plotly::plot_ly(bins, x = ~lo + 0.125, y = ~n, type = "bar", customdata = ~range,
                          name = "nearest centre", showlegend = FALSE,
                          marker = list(color = "#999999"),
                          hovertemplate = "%{customdata}, %{y} hexagons") |>
  plotly::add_lines(x = c(near_med, near_med), y = c(0, max(bins$n)), line = median_line,
                    name = "median", showlegend = FALSE, hovertemplate = median_hover,
                    inherit = FALSE) |>
  plotly::layout(yaxis = list(title = "hexagons"), bargap = 0.05)

plotly::subplot(p_decay, p_near, nrows = 2, shareX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE,
                heights = c(0.65, 0.35), margin = 0.04) |>
  plotly::layout(
    hovermode = "x unified",
    xaxis = list(title = "network distance d (km)", range = c(0, 10), hoverformat = ".2f"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"),
    margin = list(t = 120),
    annotations = list(list(xref = "x", yref = "y2", x = near_med, y = max(bins$n),
                            xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
                            bgcolor = "rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85)",
                            text = sprintf(paste0("  median distance from a hexagon<br>",
                                                  "  to its nearest centre: %.1f km"), near_med))))
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: kernel-chart
#| eval: false
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
plot_ly(); add_lines(x, y, name, line, hovertemplate)     # plotly
add_markers(x, y, marker); count(x, ...)                  # plotly, dplyr
subplot(..., nrows, shareX, heights); layout(...)         # plotly
```

- `k_cheng` is the width of the Gaussian kernel of Cheng et al. (2016), chosen so that the weight at
  the edge of the catchment is 0.05: $e^{-25/k} = 0.05$ gives $k = 25 / \ln 20
  = `r round(k_cheng, 2)` \text{ km}^2$.
- `near` is the distance from each of the 2,966 hexagons to its nearest centre.
- `near_med` is the median of `near`.
- Each element of `kernels` is one kernel, written as a function of the distance $d$. The
  Epanechnikov kernel is drawn without its factor 3/4. The power function is capped at 1. With these
  two changes, every kernel has the value 1 at a distance of 0. The factor 3/4 and the cap apply to
  the chart only. In section 4.3, the power function is computed without a cap. In KD2SFCA, the
  factor 3/4 cancels between step 1 and step 2.
- `add_lines()` draws each kernel from 0 to 10 km, twice the catchment of 5 km. The median distance
  is added to the distances, so that the hover text shows the weight at the median.
- `add_markers()` adds a dot on each kernel at the median distance.
- The kernels of the chapter's code, Hansen with `power = 2` and KD2SFCA in `ac()`, are drawn thick.
  2SFCA is dashed.
- `count()` counts the hexagons in bins of 0.25 km.
- `plot_ly(type = "bar")` draws the counts.
- A second `add_lines()` in each panel draws the dotted line at the median distance.
- `subplot(shareX = TRUE)` places the histogram under the kernels, on one distance axis.
- `hovermode = "x unified"` shows the weight of every kernel at the distance under the mouse.
:::
:::

The median distance from a hexagon to its nearest centre is `r round(near_med, 1)` km.
At `r round(near_med, 1)` km, the KD2SFCA kernel of `ac()` is `r sci(exp(-near_med^2))`, and the
Hansen weight with `power = 2` is `r sci(exp(-2 * near_med))`. At the same distance, the
Epanechnikov kernel of the readings is `r round(1 - (near_med / 5)^2, 2)`, and the Gaussian kernel
of Cheng et al. is `r round(exp(-near_med^2 / k_cheng), 2)`. The kernel of `ac()` is 0.018 at 2 km,
so the centres between 2 and 5 km away have weights below 0.018.

The kernel of `ac()` is applied to the distances in the unit of the matrix, with no conversion. A
centre 2 km away has a weight of 0.018 with distances in kilometres and a weight of 0 with distances
in metres. The kernel of Cheng et al. (2016) divides the squared distance by a width $k$ set from
the size of the catchment, so its weights are the same in kilometres and in metres.

## Hansen model: exponential versus power decay, and unequal capacities

In section 3.1, Hansen's measure was computed with `power = 2`. In the chapter's single code chunk,
the calculation is repeated with `power = 0.5`. The scores for `power = 2` and `power = 0.5` are not
compared. Luo and Wang (2003, Table 1) computed their gravity measure with seven values of $\beta$,
from 1.0 to 2.2, and found a larger variance of the scores with a larger $\beta$. Hansen (1959)
measured one exponent for each trip purpose: 2.20 for work trips, 2.35 for social trips and 3.00 for
shopping trips, with travel time in minutes (p. 9). He considered the relative measures of
accessibility "not particularly sensitive to small variations in the exponent of distance" (p. 35).
On slide 19, the exponent of distance in Stewart's model, written $\alpha$, is "usually between 1
and 2". In `ac()`, `power` is the $\beta$ of an exponential function, whereas Hansen (1959) used a
power function of distance (section 4.2).

In all six readings that compute a measure, the supply differs between locations: the jobs, retail
sales or population of each zone in Hansen (1959), the physicians at each location in Luo and Wang
(2003) and Luo and Qi (2009), the physicians of each hospital in Polzin et al. (2014), the
practising doctors of each hospital in Cheng et al. (2016) and the beds of each hospital in
Kalogirou and Foley (2006). In chapter 17, every centre has a capacity of 100, so `ac()` is not run
with unequal capacities. Testing `ac()` with unequal capacities is an extension of the course
material, based on the source of `ac()` printed in section 4.2.

The question for this section is how much the choice of decay changes the ranking of the hexagons,
and whether `ac()` weights each centre by its own capacity.

```{r}
hansen <- tibble(
  `exp(-2d)` = ac(p100, n100, D, power = 2, family = "Hansen"),
  `exp(-0.5d)` = ac(p100, n100, D, power = 0.5, family = "Hansen"),
  `1/d²` = as.vector(D^-2 %*% n100))

cor(hansen, method = "spearman") |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- The first two columns are the chapter's two calls. The third column is the power function of slide
  19 with $\alpha = 2$: `D^-2` raises every distance to the power -2, and the matrix product `%*%`
  with the capacities sums $n_j / d_{ij}^2$ over the centres for each hexagon.
- `cor(method = "spearman")` correlates the ranks of the hexagons under each pair of measures.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
h_spread <- map_dbl(hansen, \(x) max(x) / median(x))
```

The ranks are similar under the three measures, with rank correlations of 0.95 to 0.99. The spread
of the scores differs: the highest score is `r format(round(h_spread[1]), big.mark = ",")` times the
median with `power = 2`, `r round(h_spread[2])` times with `power = 0.5`, and `r round(h_spread[3])`
times with $1/d^2$. With `power = 2`, a centre 700 m away has a quarter of the weight of a centre
next to the hexagon, since $e^{-1.4} = 0.25$. With `power = 2`, a map with ten equal intervals would
place `r round(100 * mean(hansen$"exp(-2d)" < max(hansen$"exp(-2d)") / 10))`% of the hexagons in the
lowest class.

```{r}
#| echo: false
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ac(p100, n100, D, power = 2, family = "SAM"), hansen$`1/d²` / 100)))
```

With a demand of 100 in every hexagon and `power = 2`, the SAM scores of the 2,966 hexagons equal
the `1/d²` column divided by 100. The hexagons therefore have the same rank order under SAM and
under the Hansen measure with $1/d^2$.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
hex_ok <- filter(hexagons, od_ok)

decile_map <- function(data, var, title, palette = "brewer.blues") {
  tm_shape(hexagons, bbox = mapex) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "grey85", col_alpha = 0) +
  tm_shape(data) +
    tm_polygons(fill = var,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10,
                                                values = palette),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE),
                col_alpha = 0) +
    tm_title(title, size = 0.9) +
    tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
}

tmap_arrange(
  decile_map(bind_cols(hex_ok, hansen), "exp(-2d)", "Hansen, exp(-2d)"),
  decile_map(bind_cols(hex_ok, hansen), "exp(-0.5d)", "Hansen, exp(-0.5d)"),
  decile_map(bind_cols(hex_ok, hansen), "1/d²", "Power function, 1/d²"),
  ncol = 3)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `decile_map()` draws all hexagons in grey, then the valid hexagons coloured by deciles of one
  score, with no legend, so that several maps can be compared by pattern. The 159 hexagons of
  section 4.1 stay grey.
- `tmap_arrange()` places the three maps in one row.
:::

Drawn in deciles, the three maps are close to identical, as the rank correlations indicate. The
choice of decay changes the size of the differences between hexagons, and the deciles keep only
their order.

The capacity argument `n` of `ac()` has one value per centre. In the source printed in section 4.2,
the Hansen family computes `n * exp(-power * D)`. `D` is a matrix with one row per hexagon, and `n`
has one value per centre. R multiplies a matrix by a vector element by element, down the columns,
starting the vector again from its first value when the vector is shorter than the matrix. The first
value of `n` is therefore applied to the weight of the first hexagon for centre 1, the second value
to the weight of the second hexagon for centre 1, and each later value to the weight of the next
hexagon. The capacity of centre $j$ should multiply every weight for centre $j$.

The example of section 3.2.1 has four hexagons and two centres, with a capacity of 1 for centre A
and 3 for centre B:

```{r}
tibble(hexagon = 1:4,
       `ac(family = "Hansen")` = ac(toy_p, toy_n, toy_D, power = 0.5,
                                    family = "Hansen"),
       `by hand` = as.vector(exp(-0.5 * toy_D) %*% toy_n)) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `exp(-0.5 * toy_D) %*% toy_n` is the matrix product: for each hexagon, the sum over the centres of
  the weight times the capacity of that centre.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
toy_h <- ac(toy_p, toy_n, toy_D, power = 0.5, family = "Hansen")
toy_hand <- as.vector(exp(-0.5 * toy_D) %*% toy_n)
```

Hexagons 2 and 3 have swapped distances: each is 2 km from one centre and 4 km from the other.
Hexagon 3 is 2 km from the larger centre B and should score higher, as it does by hand
(`r round(toy_hand[3], 2)` against `r round(toy_hand[2], 2)`). `ac()` gives the opposite order
(`r round(toy_h[3], 2)` against `r round(toy_h[2], 2)`). The chapter's scores are correct, because
every centre has a capacity of 100. With actual capacities, the Hansen family of `ac()` gives wrong
scores. The matrix product above is the correct calculation. The 2SFCA and KD2SFCA families of
`ac()` divide by `colSums()` and transpose the weight matrix before multiplying it by the
capacities. For the toy example of section 3.2.1, with the same unequal capacities, 2SFCA gives the
same result by hand and with `ac()`.

## Floating catchment methods: kernel shape and catchment size

In section 3.2, KD2SFCA was computed once, with the kernel of `ac()` and a catchment of 5 km. The
kernel gives weights below 0.018 beyond 2 km (section 4.2). In 2SFCA (slides 24 to 26), every centre
within the catchment counts equally. In E2SFCA (slides 27 and 28), the catchment is divided into
three zones with decreasing weights. In KD2SFCA (Polzin et al., 2014), a continuous kernel replaces
the zones.

Luo and Wang (2003) computed 2SFCA with seven catchments, from 20 to 50 minutes, and found that the
scores had a lower variance with a larger catchment. Luo and Qi (2009) computed E2SFCA with two sets
of zone weights. On p. 1104, they report that 2SFCA gives higher scores than E2SFCA in areas of poor
access, which they attribute to the assumption of equal access inside the catchment in 2SFCA. They
also find that 2SFCA identifies a smaller total shortage area than E2SFCA. With the weights of set
2, which decrease faster with distance, E2SFCA identifies a larger total shortage area than with the
weights of set 1 (Luo and Qi, 2009, p. 1104; speaker notes of slide 28). Polzin et al. (2014)
compared the Epanechnikov kernel of Dai and Wang (2011) with a quartic kernel. Cheng et al. (2016)
set the width of a Gaussian kernel so that the weight at the edge of the catchment is 0.05.

Luo and Wang (2003) show that, in 2SFCA, the average accessibility weighted by demand equals the
total supply divided by the total demand, provided every centre has some demand within its
catchment. The capacity of each centre is allocated to the hexagons in its catchment. In E2SFCA and
KD2SFCA, the same weights enter step 1 and step 2, so the capacity is allocated in the same way, and
the same equality holds.

The question for this section is how much the scores depend on the kernel and on the size of the
catchment, and whether each computation satisfies the property of Luo and Wang (2003).

```{r}
fca_weights <- function(D, kernel, d0 = 5) {
  W <- switch(kernel,
    step = (D <= d0) * 1,
    ac_default = exp(-D^2) * (D <= d0),
    epanechnikov = (1 - (D / d0)^2) * (D <= d0),
    cheng = exp(-D^2 / (d0^2 / log(20))) * (D <= d0),
    e2sfca_1 = c(1, 0.68, 0.22, 0)[findInterval(D, c(d0 / 3, 2 * d0 / 3, d0),
                                                left.open = TRUE) + 1],
    e2sfca_2 = c(1, 0.42, 0.09, 0)[findInterval(D, c(d0 / 3, 2 * d0 / 3, d0),
                                                left.open = TRUE) + 1])
  matrix(W, nrow = nrow(D))
}

fca <- function(p, n, D, kernel, d0 = 5) {
  W <- fca_weights(D, kernel, d0)
  R <- n / colSums(p * W)
  R[!is.finite(R)] <- 0
  as.vector(W %*% R)
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `fca_weights()` returns a matrix of the same shape as `D`, with the weight of each pair under one
  kernel. `(D <= d0)` is `TRUE` inside the catchment and `FALSE` outside, which become 1 and 0 when
  multiplied. For E2SFCA, `findInterval()` returns 0, 1, 2 or 3 for a distance in the first, second
  or third zone or beyond the catchment. The weight is then looked up in a vector of four zone
  weights. The zones are thirds of the catchment, in place of the 10-minute zones of a 30-minute
  catchment on slide 27. The zone weights of `e2sfca_1` and `e2sfca_2` are weight sets 1 and 2 of
  Luo and Qi (2009).
- `fca()` computes the two steps of section 3.2.1 with any kernel. `colSums(p * W)` is the weighted
  demand in the catchment of each centre (`p * W` multiplies row $i$ of `W` by the demand of hexagon
  $i$), and `R` is the ratio of capacity to weighted demand for each centre. For a centre with no
  demand in its catchment, the ratio is capacity divided by 0, and is set to 0, as in `ac()`. The
  matrix product `W %*% R` is step 2, the weighted sum of the ratios for each hexagon.
:::

```{r}
fca_scores <- tibble(
  `2SFCA` = fca(p100, n100, D, "step"),
  `E2SFCA, weights 1` = fca(p100, n100, D, "e2sfca_1"),
  `E2SFCA, weights 2` = fca(p100, n100, D, "e2sfca_2"),
  `KD2SFCA, ac() kernel` = fca(p100, n100, D, "ac_default"),
  `KD2SFCA, Epanechnikov` = fca(p100, n100, D, "epanechnikov"),
  `KD2SFCA, Cheng et al.` = fca(p100, n100, D, "cheng"))

c(same_as_ac_2SFCA = all.equal(fca_scores$`2SFCA`,
                               ac(p100, n100, D, d0 = 5, family = "2SFCA")),
  same_as_ac_KD2SFCA = all.equal(fca_scores$`KD2SFCA, ac() kernel`,
                                 ac(p100, n100, D, d0 = 5, power = 2,
                                    family = "KD2SFCA")))
```

`fca()` reproduces the scores of `ac()` for 2SFCA and KD2SFCA. The table lists, for each method, the
weighted mean of the property of Luo and Wang (2003), with three other summaries:

```{r}
fca_scores |>
  summarise(across(everything(),
                   list(weighted_mean = \(a) weighted.mean(a, p100),
                        sd = sd,
                        zeros = \(a) sum(a == 0),
                        max = max))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = c("method", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "(.*)_(weighted_mean|sd|zeros|max)") |>
  kable(digits = 4)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `summarise(across())` computes four statistics for every column: the mean weighted by demand, the
  standard deviation, the number of hexagons with a score of 0, and the maximum. `pivot_longer()`
  with `names_pattern` splits each column name into the method and the statistic, so that each
  method is one row.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
sp_ratio <- sum(n100) / sum(p100)
```

The total capacity is 120 × 100 = 12,000 and the total demand
is `r format(length(p100), big.mark = ",")` × 100, so the ratio is `r round(sp_ratio, 4)`. Every
method has a weighted mean equal to that ratio, the property of Luo and Wang (2003), which is
consistent with every centre having some demand within 5 km. Every method has the
same `r format(sum(fca_scores$"2SFCA" == 0), big.mark = ",")` hexagons at zero, since every method
uses the catchment of 5 km. The scores from the kernel of `ac()` have more than twice the standard
deviation of the scores from the Epanechnikov and Gaussian kernels. The weights of the `ac()` kernel
fall to 0.37 at 1 km and 0.018 at 2 km, so its scores are concentrated on hexagons near a centre.

```{r}
#| echo: false
all_2sfca <- fca(hexagons$demand, n100, distmat_km, "step")
top_2sfca <- hexagons$fid[which.max(all_2sfca)]
```

When the 2SFCA scores are computed on all 3,125 hexagons, including the 159 hexagons of section 4.1,
the highest score, `r round(max(all_2sfca), 2)`, is at hexagon `r top_2sfca`, which has all 120
centres at a repeated distance of 4.97 km.

```{r}
fca_scores |>
  filter(`2SFCA` > 0) |>
  cor(method = "spearman") |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- The `r format(sum(fca_scores$"2SFCA" == 0), big.mark = ",")` hexagons with a score of 0 under
  every method are left out. Tied at the bottom of every ranking, they would raise all the
  correlations.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
fca_cor <- fca_scores |> filter(`2SFCA` > 0) |> cor(method = "spearman")
```

Among the hexagons with a centre within 5 km, the rank correlations among 2SFCA, E2SFCA and the
Epanechnikov and Gaussian kernels of KD2SFCA range from `r round(min(fca_cor[-4, -4]), 2)`
to `r round(max(fca_cor[-4, -4][fca_cor[-4, -4] < 1]), 2)`. The scores from the kernel of `ac()`
have their lowest rank correlation with the 2SFCA scores, `r round(fca_cor[4, 1], 2)`.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 9
fca_sf <- bind_cols(hex_ok, fca_scores)
tmap_arrange(
  decile_map(fca_sf, "2SFCA", "2SFCA, 5 km"),
  decile_map(fca_sf, "E2SFCA, weights 2", "E2SFCA, weights 2"),
  decile_map(fca_sf, "KD2SFCA, ac() kernel", "KD2SFCA, kernel of ac()"),
  decile_map(fca_sf, "KD2SFCA, Cheng et al.", "KD2SFCA, Gaussian of Cheng et al."),
  ncol = 2)
```

Under 2SFCA, the scores change in steps, at the distances where a centre enters or leaves the
catchment of a hexagon. E2SFCA has three smaller steps per centre. The scores under the Gaussian
kernel of Cheng et al. (2016) decline smoothly from each centre. The scores from the kernel of
`ac()` are highest within 1 km of a centre, where the weight is at least 0.37, and the weight is
below 0.018 at more than 2 km from a centre.

Luo and Wang (2003) tested catchments of 20 to 50 minutes for physicians. Users of eldercare may
travel less far than patients of a physician, and a smaller catchment is then plausible. The table
lists the results for catchments of 2 to 15 km:

```{r}
map_dfr(c(2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 15), \(d0) {
  a <- fca(p100, n100, D, "step", d0)
  tibble(d0_km = d0,
         sd = sd(a),
         hexagons_at_zero = sum(a == 0),
         centres_without_demand = sum(colSums(D <= d0) == 0),
         weighted_mean = weighted.mean(a, p100))
}) |>
  kable(digits = 4)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `map_dfr()` runs 2SFCA for each catchment size and stacks the one-row summaries.
  `centres_without_demand` counts the centres with no hexagon within `d0`. The capacity of those
  centres is lost in step 1, and the weighted mean falls below the ratio of supply to demand.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
lost_j <- which(colSums(D <= 3) == 0)
zero_2 <- sum(fca(p100, n100, D, "step", 2) == 0)
zero_15 <- sum(fca(p100, n100, D, "step", 15) == 0)
h_line <- which(ok)[which.min(euclid_km[ok, lost_j])]      # nearest centroid in a straight line
h_road <- which(ok)[which.min(D[, lost_j])]               # nearest hexagon by road
n_close <- sum(euclid_km[ok, ] < 0.5)
n_detour <- sum(euclid_km[ok, ] < 0.5 & D > 2)
```

The standard deviation falls as the catchment grows, as Luo and Wang (2003) found. The share of
hexagons with a 2SFCA score of 0 falls from `r round(100 * zero_2 / nrow(D))`% at 2 km
to `r round(100 * zero_15 / nrow(D))`% at 15 km. With a 2 or 3 km catchment, one centre has no
hexagon within the catchment. Its capacity is lost, so the weighted mean is below the ratio of
supply to demand. That centre, with postal code `r eldercare$ADDRESSPOS[lost_j]`, has no hexagon
within 3 km by road, although the centroid of hexagon `r hexagons$fid[h_line]`
is `r round(euclid_km[h_line, lost_j] * 1000)` m away in a straight line (map below).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6.5
dt_hex <- hexagons[h_line, ]
dt_pts <- st_sf(label = c(sprintf("centroid of hexagon %d", dt_hex$fid),
                          sprintf("eldercare centre %s", eldercare$ADDRESSPOS[lost_j])),
                geometry = c(st_centroid(st_geometry(dt_hex)), st_geometry(eldercare[lost_j, ])))
dt_link <- st_sf(label = sprintf("%.0f m in a straight line; %.1f km by road",
                                 euclid_km[h_line, lost_j] * 1000, distmat_km[h_line, lost_j]),
                 geometry = st_cast(st_union(st_geometry(dt_pts)), "LINESTRING"))
dt_note <- st_sf(label = dt_link$label,
                 geometry = st_centroid(st_geometry(dt_link)) + c(185, 0), crs = 3414)
lost_od <- ODMatrix |>
  filter(origin_id == dt_hex$fid, destination_id == eldercare$fid[lost_j])
tm_basemap("OpenStreetMap", zoom = 17) +
tm_shape(dt_hex, bbox = st_bbox(st_buffer(st_geometry(dt_hex), 120))) +
  tm_borders(col = "darkgreen", lwd = 3) +
tm_shape(dt_link) +
  tm_lines(col = "#08519c", lwd = 3, lty = "dashed") +
tm_shape(dt_note) +
  tm_text("label", size = 0.85, fontface = "bold", col = "#08519c", bgcol = "white",
          bgcol_alpha = 0.9) +
tm_shape(dt_pts) +
  tm_dots(fill = "label", size = 0.9,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c("darkgreen", "#3182bd")),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "")) +
  tm_title(sprintf("Hexagon %d and eldercare centre %s on the street map", dt_hex$fid,
                   eldercare$ADDRESSPOS[lost_j])) +
  tm_credits("Base map © OpenStreetMap contributors", position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE, legend.outside = TRUE, legend.outside.position = "bottom")
```

On the street map, the eldercare centre and the centroid of hexagon `r dt_hex$fid` are in the same
housing estate, north of the Pan-Island Expressway. The centre and the centroid are connected by
footpaths and Pipit Road. The `exit_cost` of the centre, from the nearest road to the centre,
is `r round(lost_od$exit_cost)` m, and the road closest to the centre on the street map is the
expressway. An `exit_cost` of `r round(lost_od$exit_cost)` m and a `network_cost`
of `r format(round(lost_od$network_cost), big.mark = ",")` m are consistent with a network analysis
that joined the centre to the expressway, so that the route to the centre runs along the expressway.

Of the `r n_close` pairs of hexagon and centre less than 500 m apart in a straight line in the whole
matrix, `r n_detour` are more than 2 km apart by road.

## Demand: residents aged 65 and over by areal weighting

In section 2.3.3, every hexagon was given a demand of 100. According to the chapter, the actual
demand should be used in practice. Kalogirou and Foley (2006) measured the demand for hospitals by
the population aged 65 and over, as "the population sub-group who would be most likely to be the
heaviest users". Luo and Wang (2003) and Luo and Qi (2009) took the demand from census counts of the
population. Polzin et al. (2014) adjusted the census counts with a health needs index that includes
the share of the population under 15 and over 65. In this exercise, the demand for eldercare is
measured by the residents aged 65 and over, as in Kalogirou and Foley (2006).

Exercise 1 used the 2020 census table of residents by subzone, age and sex from SingStat. The census
counts residents by subzone, and the measures require a count for each hexagon. Areal weighting
divides the count of each subzone among the hexagons in proportion to the area of the subzone that
each hexagon covers. The method assumes that the residents are spread evenly over each subzone.

The question for this section is how much the accessibility scores change when the demand is the
number of residents aged 65 and over in each hexagon.

```{r}
popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respop_census2020_agesex.csv",
                    col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

to_count <- function(x) {
  x <- str_replace_all(x, ",", "")
  x[x == "-"] <- "0"
  as.numeric(x)
}

aged_sz <- popdata |>
  mutate(across(-Number, to_count)) |>
  filter(!str_detect(toupper(Number), "^TOTAL$| ?- ?TOTAL$")) |>
  mutate(SUBZONE_N = toupper(str_trim(Number)),
         SUBZONE_N = if_else(str_starts(SUBZONE_N, "LAKESIDE"), "LAKESIDE", SUBZONE_N),
         AGED = Total_65_69 + Total_70_74 + Total_75_79 +
                Total_80_84 + Total_85_89 + Total_90andOver) |>
  group_by(SUBZONE_N) |>
  summarise(AGED = sum(AGED))

c(census_total = sum(aged_sz$AGED),
  matched_to_mp14 = sum(aged_sz$AGED[aged_sz$SUBZONE_N %in% mpsz$SUBZONE_N]))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `col_types = cols(.default = "c")` reads every column as text. As in Exercise 1, SingStat writes a
  nil or suppressed count as `-`. `to_count()` removes thousands separators, turns `-` into 0 and
  converts the text to numbers.
- The table has a row for the whole country, a row for each planning area (its name ends in " -
  Total"), and a row for each subzone. The regular expression drops the row for the whole country
  and the planning-area rows. One planning-area row is written "Changi- Total", without the space,
  and `" ?- ?TOTAL$"` matches it as well.
- The census of 2020 uses the subzones of the 2019 Master Plan, and the boundaries on this page are
  those of the 2014 Master Plan. The census subzones "Lakeside (Business)" and "Lakeside (Leisure)"
  are one subzone, "Lakeside", in the 2014 plan, and their counts are added together.
- `AGED` is the sum of the six age bands from 65 upwards.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
aged_lost <- aged_sz |> filter(!SUBZONE_N %in% mpsz$SUBZONE_N, AGED > 0)
```

The census counts `r format(sum(aged_sz$AGED), big.mark = ",")` residents aged 65 and over. All
but `r sum(aged_lost$AGED)` of them live in subzones whose names appear in the 2014 boundaries. The
other `r sum(aged_lost$AGED)` residents live
in `r paste(str_to_title(aged_lost$SUBZONE_N), collapse = " and ")`, two subzones of the 2019 plan
with no subzone of the same name in the 2014 plan.

```{r}
aged_poly <- mpsz |>
  left_join(aged_sz, by = "SUBZONE_N") |>
  mutate(AGED = replace_na(AGED, 0)) |>
  select(AGED)

hexagons$aged <- st_interpolate_aw(aged_poly, hexagons,
                                   extensive = TRUE)$AGED

c(aged_in_hexagons = sum(hexagons$aged),
  hexagons_without_aged = sum(hexagons$aged == 0))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
st_interpolate_aw(x, to, extensive = TRUE)                # sf
```

- `st_interpolate_aw()` intersects the subzones with the hexagons, and assigns each piece the share
  of the subzone's count equal to its share of the subzone's area. `extensive = TRUE` treats the
  count as a total to be divided among the pieces. The pieces of each hexagon are then added up. The
  result has one row per hexagon, in the order of `hexagons`.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
aged_share <- sum(hexagons$aged) / sum(aged_poly$AGED)
aged_zero <- sum(hexagons$aged == 0)
```

The hexagons contain `r round(100 * aged_share, 1)`% of the residents aged 65 and over. The
remaining residents live in the parts of subzones that the hexagons do not cover, on the offshore
islands and along the coast. In total, `r format(aged_zero, big.mark = ",")` hexagons have no
resident aged 65 and over, because they are in subzones with none: the water catchment areas, the
airport, the industrial estates of the west and the port.

With this demand, SAM divides by zero in those hexagons:

```{r}
p_aged <- hexagons$aged[ok]
sam_aged <- ac(p_aged, n100, D, power = 2, family = "SAM")
c(infinite = sum(is.infinite(sam_aged)),
  hexagons_with_aged = sum(p_aged > 0))
```

KD2SFCA with the kernel of Cheng et al. (2016) does not divide by the demand of the hexagon itself.
A hexagon with no demand adds nothing to the denominator of the first step. In the second step, it
has the score of the centres around it. With a capacity of 1 for each centre, the score is the
number of centres per resident aged 65 and over within 5 km, weighted by the kernel and multiplied
by 10,000:

```{r}
kd_aged <- fca(p_aged, rep(1, length(n100)), D, "cheng") * 1e4

c(national_ratio = 1e4 * length(n100) / sum(p_aged),
  weighted_mean = weighted.mean(kd_aged, p_aged))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
nat_ratio <- 1e4 * length(n100) / sum(p_aged)
kd_const <- fca_scores$`KD2SFCA, Cheng et al.`
R_const <- 1 / colSums(100 * fca_weights(D, "cheng"))
R_aged <- 1 / colSums(p_aged * fca_weights(D, "cheng"))
```

The mean of the hexagon scores, weighted by demand, is `r round(nat_ratio, 2)` centres per 10,000
residents aged 65 and over, which equals the national ratio, as Luo and Wang (2003) predict.

```{r}
#| echo: false
nz <- kd_const > 0
```

The scores range from 0 to `r round(max(kd_aged), 1)` centres per 10,000 residents aged 65 and over.
Among the planning areas with more than 5,000 residents aged 65 and over, the table lists the five
with the lowest and the five with the highest weighted mean score:

```{r}
pa_summary <- tibble(planning_area = st_join(hexagons, mpsz["PLN_AREA_N"],
                                             join = st_intersects,
                                             largest = TRUE)$PLN_AREA_N[ok],
                     aged = p_aged, acc = kd_aged) |>
  group_by(planning_area) |>
  summarise(per_10k_aged = weighted.mean(acc, aged),
            aged_65 = round(sum(aged))) |>
  filter(aged_65 > 5000) |>
  arrange(per_10k_aged)

bind_rows(head(pa_summary, 5), tail(pa_summary, 5)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- Each hexagon is assigned to the planning area it overlaps most, as in section 4.6. The score of a
  planning area is the mean of the scores of its hexagons, weighted by their residents aged 65 and
  over. `head()` and `tail()` keep the five planning areas with the lowest scores and the five with
  the highest.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Map

```{r}
#| label: aged-kd-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6
pa_named <- bind_rows(head(pa_summary, 5), tail(pa_summary, 5))
pa_lab <- label_areas(pa_named$planning_area) |>
  left_join(pa_named, by = c(PLN_AREA_N = "planning_area")) |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("%s %.2f", str_to_title(PLN_AREA_N), per_10k_aged))
tm_shape(hexagons, bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey85", col_alpha = 0) +
tm_shape(mutate(hex_ok, kd_aged = kd_aged)) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "kd_aged",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 10, Inf) * nat_ratio / 2,
                values = "brewer.rd_yl_bu", midpoint = nat_ratio),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Centres per 10,000\nresidents aged 65+"),
              col_alpha = 0) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.15, fill = "black") +
tm_shape(pa_lab) +
  tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 1.2) +
  tm_labels("label", size = 0.7, fontface = "bold", bgcol = "white", bgcol_alpha = 0.85,
            options = opt_tm_labels(point.label = TRUE)) +
  tm_title("KD2SFCA (Cheng et al. kernel, 5 km), demand = residents aged 65 and over") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: aged-kd-map
#| eval: false
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- The labelled planning areas are the ten of the table, with the score of each.
- The class breaks are multiples of the national ratio, from 0 to 5 times, with the midpoint of the
  diverging palette at the national ratio. Red hexagons have a score below the national ratio, and
  blue hexagons a score above it.
:::
:::

The highest scores are in Bukit Merah, Kallang and Toa Payoh, near the city centre,
with `r paste(round(rev(tail(pa_summary$per_10k_aged, 3)), 1), collapse = ", ")` centres per 10,000
residents aged 65 and over. Sembawang, Pasir Ris and Bukit Panjang have scores
of `r paste(round(head(pa_summary$per_10k_aged, 3), 2), collapse = ", ")`, below a third of the
national ratio of `r round(nat_ratio, 2)`.

The rank correlation between the scores under the census demand and the scores under a constant
demand, over the `r format(sum(nz), big.mark = ",")` hexagons with a score above 0,
is `r round(cor(kd_const[nz], kd_aged[nz], method = "spearman"), 2)`: the ranking of the hexagons is
almost unchanged. The ratios $R_j$ of the centres change more, with a rank correlation
of `r round(cor(R_const, R_aged, method = "spearman"), 2)` between the census demand and the
constant demand. The ratio of a centre is its capacity divided by the weighted demand in its
catchment, so a centre with many residents aged 65 and over within 5 km has a lower ratio under the
census demand than under a constant demand.

## Regional aggregation: one region per hexagon and population weights

In section 3, the regions were compared with boxplots of the hexagon scores, after a join by
`st_intersects` that counts a hexagon in every subzone it touches. Long (2017, section 4) describes
the aggregation of accessibility to regions, and warns that the aggregation is subject to the
ecological fallacy and the modifiable areal unit problem. Luo and Wang (2003) weight the average of
the accessibility scores by population. Luo and Qi (2009, Table 1) count the population of the areas
whose ratio is below the shortage standard of 1 physician per 3,500 residents. The readings contain
no shortage standard for eldercare centres. The threshold in this exercise, half the national ratio
of centres to residents aged 65 and over, is an extension of the course material.

The question for this section is how the five regions compare when each hexagon counts once, and
each resident aged 65 and over counts equally.

```{r}
hexagons$REGION_N <- st_join(hexagons, mpsz["REGION_N"],
                             join = st_intersects, largest = TRUE)$REGION_N
nrow(hexagons)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `largest = TRUE` keeps, for each hexagon, only the subzone it overlaps most, so the join returns
  one row per hexagon.
:::

```{r}
eldercare$REGION_N <- st_join(eldercare, mpsz["REGION_N"])$REGION_N

region_summary <- tibble(region = hexagons$REGION_N[ok],
                         aged = p_aged,
                         acc = kd_aged,
                         reach = colSums(t(D) <= 5) > 0) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(hexagons = n(),
            aged_65 = round(sum(aged)),
            per_10k_aged = weighted.mean(acc, aged),
            aged_no_centre_5km = sum(aged[!reach]) / sum(aged),
            aged_below_half_national = sum(aged[acc < nat_ratio / 2]) / sum(aged)) |>
  left_join(count(st_drop_geometry(eldercare), REGION_N, name = "centres"),
            by = c(region = "REGION_N"))

kable(region_summary, digits = 3)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `reach` is `TRUE` for a hexagon with at least one centre within 5 km by road. `t()` transposes the
  matrix, one column per hexagon, so `colSums(t(D) <= 5)` counts the centres within 5 km of each
  hexagon.
- `per_10k_aged` is the mean score of the region weighted by the residents aged 65 and over in each
  hexagon. `aged_no_centre_5km` and `aged_below_half_national` are the shares of the region's
  residents aged 65 and over who live in hexagons with no centre within 5 km, and in hexagons with a
  score below half the national ratio.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
rs <- region_summary
r_of <- \(r, v) rs[[v]][rs$region == r]
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5.5
region_map <- mpsz |>
  group_by(REGION_N) |>
  summarise() |>
  left_join(region_summary, by = c(REGION_N = "region"))
region_lab <- region_map |>
  st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON") |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  mutate(area = st_area(geometry)) |>
  group_by(REGION_N) |>
  slice_max(area, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("%s\n%.1f per 10,000\n%d centres",
                         str_to_title(REGION_N), per_10k_aged, centres))
tm_shape(region_map, bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "per_10k_aged",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 10, Inf) * nat_ratio / 2,
                values = "brewer.rd_yl_bu", midpoint = nat_ratio),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Centres per 10,000\nresidents aged 65+"),
              col = "white", lwd = 2) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.15, fill = "black") +
tm_shape(region_lab) +
  tm_text("label", size = 0.8, fontface = "bold", bgcol = "white", bgcol_alpha = 0.8) +
  tm_title("Regions: mean score weighted by residents aged 65 and over") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)
```

The Central Region has `r r_of("CENTRAL REGION", "centres")` of the 120 centres, and a score
of `r round(r_of("CENTRAL REGION", "per_10k_aged"), 1)` centres per 10,000 residents aged 65 and
over. In the other four regions, the score is
between `r round(min(rs$per_10k_aged[rs$region != "CENTRAL REGION"]), 1)`
and `r round(max(rs$per_10k_aged[rs$region != "CENTRAL REGION"]), 1)`, below the national ratio
of `r round(nat_ratio, 2)`. The North-East Region has the lowest score,
with `r format(r_of("NORTH-EAST REGION", "aged_65"), big.mark = ",")` residents aged 65 and over,
the second-largest number of the five regions, and `r r_of("NORTH-EAST REGION", "centres")` centres.
In the North Region, `r round(100 * r_of("NORTH REGION", "aged_no_centre_5km"), 1)`% of the
residents aged 65 and over live more than 5 km by road from a centre,
and `r round(100 * r_of("NORTH REGION", "aged_below_half_national"))`% live in hexagons with a score
below half the national ratio. Both shares are the largest of the five regions.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
tibble(region = hexagons$REGION_N[ok], aged = p_aged, acc = kd_aged) |>
  filter(aged >= 1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = region, y = acc, weight = aged)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = nat_ratio, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "centres per 10,000 residents aged 65+ (log scale)",
       subtitle = "Hexagons with at least one resident aged 65+, weighted by that number; dashed line: national ratio") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `aes(weight = aged)` weights each hexagon by its residents aged 65 and over, so that each hexagon
  counts in proportion to its residents aged 65 and over. A hexagon with two such residents has a
  weight of 2, and a hexagon in a housing estate a weight of several hundred.
- `scale_y_log10()` puts the scores on a logarithmic scale. The 119 hexagons with residents aged 65
  and over and a score of 0 have no logarithm, and are left out of the boxes.
:::

In this chart, each hexagon appears once. The regions are compared by one score, in centres per
10,000 residents aged 65 and over. The dashed line marks the national ratio, which is the score
every region would have if the centres were distributed in proportion to the residents aged 65 and
over.

# Reflection

In chapter 17, accessibility to eldercare centres is modelled with three measures from one function.
The three maps of Part 1 show the same pattern: high scores in the city centre and around each
eldercare centre, and low scores in the west, the reservoir areas and the far east. In Part 2, I
found that the scores depend on the distance matrix, the formula inside `ac()`, the size of the
catchment and the demand.

**The distance matrix has errors.** 159 hexagons have one distance to all 120 centres, the distance
to the last centre in the file. One of them is within 5 km of every centre in the matrix. Under
2SFCA, it was the highest-scoring hexagon until I removed the 159 hexagons. The other 158 hexagons
score 0 under KD2SFCA in Part 1. Of the 159 hexagons, 94 hexagons have a centre within 5 km in a
straight line, so their scores of 0 come from wrong distances. I found the errors by comparing the
network distances with straight-line distances. Some valid distances are also much longer than the
straight line: centre 370093 is 125 m from hexagon 2479 in a straight line and 5.6 km away by road.
With a catchment of 2 or 3 km, its capacity is lost.

**Three measures of `ac()` differ from the formulas on the slides and in the readings.** Its Hansen
measure uses an exponential decay, where Hansen (1959) used a power of distance. When the capacities
of the centres differ, the Hansen measure also multiplies the weights of one centre by the capacity
of another centre. Its KD2SFCA kernel has no width. With distances in kilometres, the weights beyond
2 km are below 0.02, so a catchment of 5 km has the effect of a catchment of about 2 km. The KD2SFCA
scores also change with the unit of distance. Its SAM does not use `d0`. It uses the demand once,
where the formula on slide 29 uses it twice. With a constant demand, its SAM equals a Hansen measure
with the power function $1/d^2$, divided by the demand. None of these differences appears in the
chapter's output. I found each difference by reading the source of `ac()`, which is about 50 lines
long.

**The floating catchment scores are a capacity per person.** The unit is the same for 2SFCA, E2SFCA
and KD2SFCA. The mean of their scores weighted by demand equals the national ratio, a property
derived by Luo and Wang (2003). Every computation of these methods with a catchment of 5 km or more
satisfies the property. With a catchment of 2 or 3 km, one centre has no hexagon within its
catchment, and the mean falls below the ratio. The Hansen and SAM scores have no unit. They can be
compared only as ranks or ratios between hexagons, as Long (2017) says of gravity-based measures.

**The demand changes the ratios of the centres more than the scores of the hexagons.** With the
residents aged 65 and over in place of a constant demand of 100, the rank correlation is 0.98 for
the hexagon scores and 0.64 for the centre ratios.

**Regions under the census demand.** With the KD2SFCA kernel of Cheng et al. (2016), the score of
every region outside the Central Region is below the national ratio. The North-East Region has the
lowest score. In the North Region, 6.5% of the residents aged 65 and over have no centre within 5 km
by road, the largest share of the five regions.

**Limits.** Every centre has a capacity of 100, because the data have no measure of the size of a
centre. Areal weighting spreads the residents of a subzone evenly over its area, including its parks
and industrial land. The census is from 2020. The records of the centres were last updated in July
2016, according to the field `FMEL_UPD_D` of the shapefile. The chapter gives no information on the
road network used for `OD_Matrix.csv`. I took the catchment of 5 km and the kernels from the chapter
and the readings, without data on how far residents aged 65 and over in Singapore travel to a
centre.

# About this document

Written and executed in Quarto with R `r getRversion()`,
`SpatialAcc` `r packageVersion("SpatialAcc")`, `sf` `r packageVersion("sf")` and
`tmap` `r packageVersion("tmap")`. All figures and tables are generated at render time from the data
in `data/`, so nothing on this page is pasted in.

I used AI assistance while working out the approach and the extensions in Part 2. The analysis was
run and checked by me.
